its Fifty-ninth Annual Communica~ipn at Golden Gate
Commandery Hall, in the City of San Francisco, on Tuesday,
the 13th day of October, A. L. 5908, at 10 o'clock a. m.

. . The Grand Master filled the vacant places by the appomtment pro tempore of R.". W.". Jacob H. Neff as
Deputy Grand Master, Georg~ Penlington as Junior Grand
Steward, and W. ·. Ca'rl Heilbron as Grand Pursuivant. He
also appoi~ted M:.
Thomas Flint to fill a vacancy in
the Committee on J unsprudence, occasioned by the inability
of Past Grand Master George W. Hunter to be presen~.

V'I!:.

7

There being a sufficient representation, the Grand
Lodge was opened in Ample Form, with music by the choir
and prayer by the Grand Chaplain.
The Grand Master read a letter from the R. ·. W. ·. Reuben H. Lloyd, Deputy Grand Master, expressing his inability to accept further favors from the Grand Lodge at this
time on account of ill health. Thereupon Brother Benjamin
F. Bledsoe introduced the following resolution:
WHEREAS, R.". W:. REUBEN HEDLEY LLOYD, Deputy Grand Master
of this Grand Lodge, is suffering from a severe illness, confined to his
bed and Ur.Jable to attend upon this Annual Communication:
AND WHEREAS, The · members of this Grand Lodge are and ever
will be deeply sensible not only of the commanding respect in which
Brother LLOYD is held throughout the great State of California, but
also of the exalted stations to which he has been raised throughout
the domain of Masonry-all the natural result of his own unswerving
stand and indefatigable labors as a loyal and enlightened citizen, and
honorable and painstaking lawyer., and a true and helpful Mason:
AND WHEREAS, In his inforced absence from this Annual Communication of this Grand Lodge, we will suffer a serious and all too
apparent loss:
Now, therefore, be it Resolved by this Grand Lodge, that we hereby
tender our heartfelt sympathy to Brother LLOYD in his present affliction,
·and hereby give expression to the hope that swells within our hearts,
that by the time another year shall have passed he will be with us
once again, to measurably lighten our labors in virtue of his own
forceful example, his helpful counsel and his most agreeable and
beneficent presence.
·

v:. w:.

And be it further Resolved that the
Grand Secretary be
instructed to transmit to Brother LLOYD at his earliest convenience a
copy of this resolution with a bouquet of flowers.
\~7hich was unanimously adopted.

following:

The Grand Master then deiivered his Annual Address
to the Grand Lodge, as follows :
T o tlze M.'. w:. Grand Lodge, Free and Accepted Masons,
iii th e State of Cai-ifomia :

The annual return of the month of OctDber has brought together
the delegated members of the Great Masonic Family of California.
A year ago when I first entered upon my duties as your Grand
Master, it was my desire to do exact and equal justice and to subserve
only the interests and honor of the Fraternity at large; what I lacked
in ability I hope I have made up in zeal and love for our beloved
Order. It has been a year quite like most years, full of hopes and
of disappointments; disappointments chiefly because our aim is high
and we are always sure to fall a little short of the standard we set
for ourselves.
In. holding the honored office of Grand Master, I have been
impressed with the Masonic growth. Its obligations have been everywhere exacted, and obedience to the moral law has been rigidly
enforced. Much as we have accomplished, much yet is to be done.
Let all our aims be our God, ou~ Country and Truth. God's love
is compatible with universal wisdom; our ·country's right is more
beautiful than affection, and Truth will brighten the sunshine. There
is joy to all men living a Masonic life. The world is upheld by the
veracity of good men; they make the earth wholesome. Right ethics
are central, and go from the soul outward. Life's victory is to gain
control of the selfish nature, that it may be subordinate to a sense
of duty, to cultivate and develop the moral faculties so that they may
assert their superiority and thereby establish in the individual true
manhood, morality being an emanation from God.
Every institution, society or order is beneficial in its ultimate
results just in proportion as it enlists, encourages and assists the
individual to fight this battle and gain this victory. Spasmodic fevers
of charity will never gain the battle of life. Character is to be found
in the permanent disposition of the mind, in the governing purpose
of the life. This purpose is the result of a deliberate, unreserved
commitment of the Spirit to the ends of worthiness. To overcome
this selfish power, it is absolutely necessary for the individual to·
commit himself fully, firmly, deliberately, unreservedly to the ends
of benevolence. What the man needs, what the interests of his moral
nature demand in this conflict with these selfish tendencies, is some
individual, some influence, some institution which will lead or induce
him to rise up to worthiness. The smallest acqoisition of such in
any quarter is so much good to the commonwealth of men.

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

A true man is himself a temple, a radiating center of influence
that tints the lives that come into its light. We have heard that
Masonry is grand because it is old; not so. Masonry is old because
it is grand. What is truth is effective, generative, makes for itself
room, food and allies. All truth and moral force is a positive good;
it goes out from you whether you will or not, and profits me, whom
you never thought of.
Masonry has withstood the ravages of time, and unrelenting
crusades against it, because it was founded upon a philosophic basis.
It has noble, grand ends to accomplish. Masonry is that Imperial
Institution whose example has actually called into being almost
every other benevolent order which exists today; it is that imperishable institution which takes by the hand the Brother who has fallen
in this battle of life, raises him to his feet again, gently brushes
from his brow the dust of defeat, and encourages him to go forth
again to the conflict with renewed strength, and a firmer determination
to accomplish something in life.
It must always be a joy to a Mason to meet and know a man
that has hoped, felt, failed, loved and lived. Masonry is that noble
Institution which in the silent watches, unobserved, carries joy and
gladness to the lonely and desolate of earth; that immovable Institution which by her tenets and cordial virtue, draws unbidden to her
sanctum-sanctorum the high, the low, the rich, the poor, and numbers
them all alike, her own plighted sons and workmen; and by its
sublime principles, unswerving faith and noble deeds challenges the
admiration of all men.
We are Masons not for what we may get, but for what we may
attain, what we may do for others. This is its glory-this is what
makes Masonry the synonym of charity in the world, will shed brightness and yet still brighter luster upon its honored name as the
centuries one by one shall be added to the past.
Those of you who have heretofore attended the Annual Communications of this Grand Lodge will be sure to miss the venerable
. form and gracious bearing of one who long commanded the profound
respect of all men; whose life was spent usefully to his fellow-men
and with devotion to his family and home ; a good, true citizen and
a thorough Mason, whose noble deeds and many virtues will long
be remembered by those who knew him. Brother Chauncey Carrol
Bush was for many years the Bible-Bearer of this Grand Lodge, and
at the last Communication it was our pleasure to reappoint him to
that honorable position. His spirit took its flight to the Higher Lodge
on the twenty-first day of December, 1907.
Brother Jacob Voorsanger, a zealous, beloved Mason, and at one
time Grand Orator of this Grand Body, has gone to render his report

before another and higher tribunal, to his Grand Master above. We
fcocl and know that his presence came as a light, love, relief and truth
being the inviolable code inscribed ever upon his standard.
Among our illustrious Brothers of other Grand Jurisdictions who
have been called from their labors on earth during the past year to
join the Grand Master above are:

I have received and answered many letters asking explanations
regarding doubtful questions, construction of laws and decisions. In

On my assuming the Office of Grand Master, I received a letter
stating that "A resident of Cavite, P. I., desired to affiliate with Cavite
Lodge, No. 350. He held papers and documents showing that he had
been a member of Lodge El Porvenir, No. 2, in Madrid, and the
'Grand Orient of Spain;' both having gone out of existence in 1891,
a bout the time the present 'Spanish Grand Orient'· was being formed,
and asking if said Lodge could legally elect him to membership."
My answer wasThat the inability of the applicant for affiHation to procure a
<limit will not stand in the way of affiliation where a satisfactory
explanation in writing of the inability to furnish same is made. (Part
III Article III Section 13 of the Constitution) .
' The only ~uestion as to the• right of Cavite Lodge to receive
the application, so far as I can see, arises because of the doubt as to
the standing of the Lodge in which the applicant was made and of
which he was a member-(El Porvenir, No. 2, in Madrid, subject
to the Grand Orient of Spain). The. Grand Lodge of California
recognizes no man as a Mason unless he has regularly been made
one in some Lodge cf Masons, acting under a Charter or Dispensation from some Grand Lodge having proper authority to grant such
Charter or Dispensation. (Vol. 10, Grand Lodge Proceedings, page
153.) I have no knowledge as to the Masonic standing of the Gra~1d
Orient of Spain, and under the circumstances I do not see how Cav1te
Lodge can be permitted to accept the application for affiliation from
this Brother.

Warden, by direction of the Master, had preferred charges of unMasonic conduct against a member of . Fresno Lodge, No. 247; that

the charges were duly presented to the Master, who called a Special

Trial Commissioners were elected and summons was served on the
nccused to appear for trial. That the Master having directed the

"When the Master of a Lodge desires to p;efer charges against
11 member of his own Lodge, the charges must be presented to the
Grand Master; and, if he finds them sufficient, he will designat~ the
l,odge in which the case shall be tried and will transmit the charges
to the Master of that Lodge-with directions to proceed to elect
Cou:imissioners for the determination thereof, in accordance with the
regulations of the Grand Lodge." (Volume 17, page 247, Grand Lodge
Proceedings.)
And, Volume XXIV, pages 645-902, Grand Lodge P roceedings:
"If the Master of a Lodge directs the Junior Warden to prefer
charges against one of its members, he cannot preside at the trial
nor should the charges be presented to him.'' Therefore, in accordance with the Constitution of the Grand Lodge, the ninth paragraph,
Section 1, Article II, Part 2, I ·appointed Las Palmas Lodge, No. 366,
to conduct the trial.
Under date of October thirtieth, 1907, I received a communication with enclosure of a circular emanating from the office of Henry
Ernest Ceoper, District Grand Master of the Grand Lodge of Scotland,
over the Territory of Hawaii, notifying the Officers and members of
Hawaii Lodge, No. 21, to be present at the election and installation
of the office bearers for the ensuing year and informing the Brethren
of Hawaii Lodg·e, No. 21, that the Jurisdiction of the Grand District
Lodge of Scotland is limited to Lodge Pacific, No. 822, and Lodge
Maui, No. 984. Said circular also adds that this action on the part
of the Grand Lodge is not to be taken as interfering in the slightest
degree with the autonomy of Lodges within the Territory of Hawaii
holding under the jurisdiction of the Grand Lodge of California, but
is in line with the general policy of the Grand Lodge of Scotland in
placing daughter Lodges under the immediate supervision of a District
Grand Lodge; the writer stating that the Fraternity is numerically
too weak in numbers to think of forming a Gra1.1d Body, but is of the
opinion that the Territory of Hawaii. being an American Territory,
that American Masonry should not only be fostered, but have some
adequate protection.
I answered that the Grand Lodge of Scotland places its Subordinate Lodges under the immediate supervision of a District Grand
Lodge, and which in no way affects the present standing of the various
Lodges in Hawaii, at present under the Jurisdiction of tbe Grand

I received a communication asking if a non-affiliated Mason whose

dimit is more than two yea.rs old, who applied for membership in this

I was asked the following: "When a Trial Commission has proceeded in the trial and found the Brother guilty, and then adjourned
without signing the findings, can the Commissioners subsequently
legally sign the same?"
'M y answer was: "That where the record will show that the
Commission met regularly, heard and weighed the evidence and rendered their judgment, that the record was properly prepared by the
Secretary and approved by the Commissioners as a correct one, I can
see no reason why their signatures would not verify the record even
if made by them individually after adjourning."
An application was made to me in April last by a Brother of

the Park hills within the city lirflits.
The Constitution of the Grand Lodge, or a Subordinate Lodge,
does not provide for a Lodge to hold a session at any other place

except in their Lodge-room, and an outdoor session is very dangerous,

I received a communication from several Lodges asking the
question, "When does a man become a member of the Lodge in this
Jurisdiction, prior to or subsequent to his signing the By-Laws of the
Lodge?" i held that · after he had received the full ceremony appertaining to the Master Masons' degree. By affiliation, after he had
been elected and his <limit from the Lodge to which he formerly belonged had been deposited in the Lodge to which he had been elected.
I find nothing in the law that makes the signing of the By-Laws a
prerequisite to becoming a member of a Lodge. The law does, however, require that every person raised to the degree of Master Mason
(except when the degree is conferred at the request of another Lodge)
"or elected to be a member thereof, shall sign the By-Laws." (Section 3, Article IV, Uniform Code of By-Laws.) And no doubt the
performance of this duty may be. required.
I received a communication asking if the daughter of a deceased
Mason who, at the time of his death, was a member in good standing
and who was living with her husband, a "profane," and a minor son,
the husband by reason of sickness or physical disability being unable
to support her, was entitled to relief from the funds of the Lodge. I
h.eld that the daughter of a Master Mason does not forfeit her rights
to be treated as such merely because she has married a man who is
not a Mason, and I know of no reason why the rule should be
different where the daughter of a Mastor Mason continues to live
with her husband (a non-Mason) . She is still the daughter of a
Master Mason and is none the less worthy of fraternal consideration
because she does not leave . her husband. Under such circumstances
the Lodge of which her father was a member may very properly grant'
her the necessary assistance to such an extent as may be reasonably
sufficient to cover her individual needs. The relief extended, however,
should be limited to such an amount as is necessary for the wife
alone. The question of the amount required for this purpose must
necessarily be left entirely to the discretion of the Lodge and its
Officers.
I received a communication from Suisun Lodge, No. 55, stating
that Brother Charles Figeley was expelled by that Lodge, March twentythird, 1907, for ti.nmasonic conduct, and pending review of his case by
the Grand Lodge died September, 1907. The Grand Lodge subsequent
to his death, on October tenth, 1907, made an order reversing the
judgment of expulsion, and remanded the case for new trial. The
question is as to the effect of such re~ersal. I held that our Constitution contemplates that no judgment of expulsion or suspension shall
become final until aftirmancc by the Grand Lodge (Section 10, Article

IV, Part 6, Constitution). While such a judgment goes into effect
at once (Section 9 of the same Article), the effect of a reversal by
the Grand Lodge is to restore the accused to all his rights and privileges as a member of the Lodge (Section 2, Article V, Part 6). If in
the meantime the accused had died, there can be no doubt that he
should be considered as having been in good standing at the time
of his death.
I received a communication from the Secretary of Howard Lodge,
No. 96, asking if a member of another Lodge can be installed as
Tyler when there is an objection. I held that the Tyler of a Lodge
need not necessarily be a member of the Lodge to which he acts as
Tyler, but must be a Master Mason in good standing. The office of
Tyler being appointive, the appointment being made by the Master,
no objection would be effective if the Master chose to appoint a
l
,
member cif another Lodge.
I received a communication from the Master of Manila Lodge,
No, 342, stating that one Lester W. Lord, having resided in the juris .
diction of Manila Lodge for over three years, was elected to receive
the degrees of Masonry in that Lodge, and the Entered Apprentice
degree was conferred upon him by Manila Lodge. That a few day
thereafter the candidate was ordered to transport service and has never
had an opportunity to visit Manila again. In due course of time he
returned to his home in West Ossipee, New Hampshire, and at his
request Manila Lodge asked Ossipee Valley Lodge, No. 74, in Ossipee,
New Hampshire, to extend the courtesy by conferring the Second and
Third Degrees upon Brother Lord.
Ossipee Valley Lodge refused to confer the degrees, claiming that
the Entered Apprentice degree conferred by Manila Lodge was illegal;
as years previous Brother Lord had been rejected to receive the degrees
of l\Iasonry in Ossipee Valley Lodge No. 74, of Ossipee, New Hampshire, and the Lodges in New Hampshire Jurisdiction claim exclusive·
and perpetual jurisdiction over a rej ected candidate. The candidate
desired to come to San Francisco, if necessary, in order to receive
the other two degrees, and the Master of Manila Lodge was not sure
whether the candidate could receive the degrees in view of the circumstances.
I held that the Grand Lodge of California recognizes perpetual
jurisdiction only when an applicant has been elected and initiated by
the Lodge to which he applied. We also recognize a jurisdiction of
one year over a rejected candidate. When the full year for a rejection
has lapsed, the jurisdiction has lapsed, and we recognize no claim or
authority over a rej ected applicant by reason of the rejection, whether
claimed by one of our own Lodges or by a Lodge in any other State
or country. This is in accordance with a decision of the Committee on
Jurisprudence. (See Proceedings of 1893, page 216.)

38

39

41

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

It is true that the facts there under consideration were different
from those in this case, but Brother Belcher and his colleagues were
declaring the law applicable on the question of perpetual jurisdcition,
and their conclusion appears to me to be the only logical one. ·
We claim the absolute right to determine as to the qualifications
of persons residing in 'the Jurisdiction of our Lodges. Under our
laws, as they are written, the Jurisdiction of Ossipee Valley Lodge,
No. 74, New Hampshire, over Brother Lord lapsed with the expiration
of one year from the date of his rejection, and any Lodge under our
Jurisdiction having in other respects the right to receive his application
for the degrees could receive it regardless of his former rejection.
Upon the facts stated, I have no doubt that the Entered Apprentice
Degree was legally conferred on Brother Lord by Manila Lodge, No.
342, and that he is now subject to the Jurisdiction of that Lodge, which
Lodge should proceed to confer the remaining degrees upon him or
request any other Lodge to confer them for it.
- Of course, no Lodge beyond our Jurisdiction can be forced to do
this for another Lodge, and it is eminently proper that some Lodge in
San Francisco be requested to do it, as is desired by the applicant.
The Grand Lodge of New Hampshire can have no just ground
of complaint against us because of our refusal to recognize any claim
by way of perpetual jurisdiction over rejected candidates.
From the lVIaster of Manila Lodge I received the following
queries:
First-In case a petition for the degrees of Masonry is received
from a person who has already received one or more degrees in
one of the various irregular Lodges in the Philippine Islands, how
should it be acted upon? Should it be. received and acted upon the
same as the petition of any other "profane," and if favorable action
is taken, should all three degrees be conferred, or should the petitioner
be "healed?"
Second-What is the exact method of procedure for "healing" in
the Jurisdiction of California?
I replied to query one that a regular Masonic Lodge does not
and cannot recognize an irregular or clandestine Lodge of Masons.
The only way to proceed is to take a petition for degrees, have it
referred to the proper committee, and if reported on favorably, a
ballot should be taken, and if elected the three degrees of Masonry
should be conferred.
Query two: "Healing" is reobliititing, but I could not find any
authority in the Constitution and Regulations of the Grand Lodge for
"healing" a so-called Mason who may pretend to have taken degrees
in a clandestine or irregular Lodge, as it is not supposed that a
regular Lodge or its members would have Masonic communication
with an irregular Lodge.

I received advices from several Lodges stating that they were in
receipt of a communication from Fredericksburg Lodge, No. 4, A. F.
& A. M., of Fredericksburg, Virginia, relative to contributing to a
lasting Masonic memorial to be erected in honor and to . the memor,.
of our illustrious Brother, George Washington, and asking if a donation
from their Lodges would be in order.
I held that there was no reason why the said communication
should not be received by the Lodges, but the funds ot a Masonic
Lodge are set apart for its necessary expenses and for such calls for
relief for which the Lodge was constituted; and no Lodge should,
C'xpend its funds for any other purpose, however worthy or patriotic
it may be. For purposes other than those recognized as purely Masonic, the members of the Lodge desiring to make a contribution
should make same from their private funds, but this appeal being
for a worthy Masonic cause, I believe it should m~et the approbation
of the Brethren to contribute individually such amounts as they may
see fit and forward in the name of the Lodge.
·1 received a communication from the Secretary of Franklin Lodge,
No. 143, stating that they had amended their By-Laws to be known
as Section 5, Article IX, which would read as follows : "Every member
of this Lodge shall pay in addition to the dues prescribed in Section l,
Article IX of the Constitution of Franklin Lodge, the sum of 15 cents
per month, payable in the same manner and at the same time as the
regular Lodge dues; said money collected in this way to be devoted
to social purposes," and asking my approval.
I replied that I could not approve same, as this amendment would
then be an enforced assessment on the members of the Lodge to
obtain money for purposes other than the Lodge was originally
constituted for.
It has been the custom for years for the various Lodges in San
Francisco to appoint a Funeral Committee each month, consisting of
three Master Masons, whose duty it is to attend the funerals of those
of our deceased Brethren belonging to various Lodges in different
parts of the State and other Jurisdictions, whose funeral ceremonies are
conducted under the auspices of the several Lodges in San Francisco.
The names arc taken alphabetically from the Roster of the different
Lodges, irrespective of whether the Brothers are in San Francisco or
elsewhere; and the attendance at the services in many cases is very
meager. I would suggest that this Grand Lodge take some measures
instructing the Master and Wardens of the various Lodges that, in
appointing a F uneral Committee, they appoint from among the members, those who are willing to serve on such committee, as it is a
duty we owe to our departed Brethren.
I received a communication from the Master of a Lodge stating
that a candidate had been initiated, passed and the first section of the

Third Degree had been conferred upon him. On his return to the
Lodge he refused to conform to the requirements 'made of him,
although told that it was a necessary part of the work and that every
Master Mason who has preceded him had been required to do so.
On his refusal he was requested to leave the Lodge, and did so. Thereafter the candidate expressed sorrow at having refused to do as
requested, and
the next regular meeting of the Lodge was allowed
to go_into the Lodge-room and apologize and say that he would now
cheerfully obey every wish of the Lodge. Some of the Brethren
wanted to proceed with the conferring of the second section, and
others claimed that he should not be allowed to go further, and asked
my opinion regarding the matter.
I advised that to discipline the candidate would probably do him
good and make a better Mason of him in the future, and that the
. conferring of the second section of the Third Degree should be
deferred for some time, or until the Brethren thought that he had
been punished enough.

In the past it has been the custom of this Grand Body to present
the incoming Grand Master with a complete set of reports · of the
Proceedings of this Grand Lodge, but owing to the great calamity
which befell this city in 1906 all of the extra Reports of the Proceedings were destroyed by fire, and as there are many questions of
Masonic law which are referred to the Grand Master to elucidate,
it will in the future be exceedingly difficult for Grand Masters who
reside in parts of the State where a complete set of the reports are
not at hand to answer such questions on Masonic law as may be
required.
·

complete reports of the Proceedings of this Grand Lodge, from its

formation, to be reprinted, and that each Lodge throughout the State
be furnished with a complete set at actual cost of printing and binding.

The Masonic Home at Decoto looks for its very existence to this
Grand Body, and from my observation it is not yet what it was
intended to be. It should be a place where more of our less fortunate
Brothers, their widows and orphans, can be taken care of, especially the
orphans.
.
I would urge that the reports and all literature available per-.
taining to the Masonic Home be read in the Lodge-room upon
occasions when there may be time, that the Fraternity at large may
become interested in the work of our Home.
Of the commendable spirit that dictates the erection of these
magnificent monuments of Masonic charity, there is nothing that can
be said, but what is complimentary of these promoters, and by bringing
before our young Masons the knowledge and advantages of this Home
it will make them zealous, intelligent ·members of the Order, and to
be that they must become interested in the work of this noble charity
where old age is brought into a friendly haven and the young lives
sheltered from poverty and vice, tenderly guarded from the tempests
of youthful temptation, unchecked by parental control.
From its chambers issue forth the peaceful faces of honorable
old age, and from the dormitories the happy youths to tell the world
what Masonry is, and God grant that Masonry may ever be a helper
to the poor and helpless, the hand-maid of the most high God.
The expense per capita is now very large, but I cannot recommend
any place where it could be curtailed or reduced, as the Institution.
now stands with its present limited accommodations.
The only way that I can see whereby the cost per capita could
be reduced would be to enlarge the Home so that we could take care
of all who are worthy of our assistance.
I would suggest that the Board of Trustees governing the Home
be reduced to seven, and that the Grand Master, the Deputy Grand
Master, the Senior and Junior Grand Wardens of this Grand Lodge
be Trustees, and that three Trustees at large be appointed to serve,
one for one year, one for two years, and one for three years ; then,
thereafter, each incoming Grand Master to appoint one, whose term
of office shall be for three years; the Grand Secretary to perform the
duty of Secretary to the Board of Trustees and the Grand Treasurer
to be the Treasurer of the fun<ls of the Home.
In this way the Grand Master and Grand Officers will have a
thorough knowledge of the workings of the Institution.
· I would further add that it should be considered a duty of every
Lodge in this Jurisdiction to have a representative visit the Home at

least once a year, and acquaint himself with the workings of the
Institution and report the result of his observ~tion to his Lodge.
I would recommend that the regulations as to the physical and
mental condition of the person nominated for admission in the Home
should be so changed that all who are worthy and in need of the care
of such a Home should be admitted, and the . admission in the Home
be in the order of their application and that no distinction or discrimination be made against any Lodge, as to the number of inmates coming

On August twenty-second last, the Very Worshipful George Johnson, Grand Secretary, requested me to appoint some one to fulfill the
duties of Grand Secretary.
Brother Johnson's continued ill h~alth made it imperative that
he resign from the office which he hau so ably filled for many years,
faithful to every trust reposed in him; and it is only an act of justice
that I now express my high .appreciation of the services rendered during
the past year and my deep sense of personal gratitude for the numerous
favors extended to me by Brother George Johnson.
'I'o our worthy, faithful Past Grand Secretary, Brother George
Johnson, let this Grand Lodge earnestly, fraternally and affectionately
express its deep gratitude for hi5 diligent, conscientious services and
with warm thanks for the past good government of his office and our
prayers for his restored health.
The correspondence of the Grand Master's Office has been quite
large. Let it be remembered that there are three hundred and fifteen
Chartered Lodges and eleven Lodges under dispensation existing in
this Jurisdiction, and it would be seen that if there is only an occasional letter from each, the labor of the Grand Master i"n answering
all must be considerable in the aggregate; and has illustrated to me
the absolute necessity of having a Grand Secretary who is conversant
with Masonic Jurisprudence, and a prompt and correct business man.
Realizing this, on August twenty-fifth, I appointed Brother John
Whicher, a Past Master and a member of King David's Lodge, No. 209,
to the important office of Grand Secretary for the unexpired term
made vacant by the resignation of Brother George Johnson.
As I am about to pass the laurels of Grand Master to another,
the.re is just a word of advice I would like to extend .

The popularity and love for our Order must be every Mason's
Jealous care. While we are pleased over the voluntary approach of
representative mtn to become one of us, yet must we be guarded in allowing only good men. I am sure that in many cases the member who
recommends candidates is not always mindful of the first injunction
given a11 Entered Apprentice Mason: "Be faithful to the trust committed to your care, and manifest your fidelity to your principles by
a strict oLservance of the Constitution of the Fraternity by adhering
to the ancient landmarks thereof; and by refusing to recommend anyone to a participation in our privileges unless you have strong reasons
to believe that by a similar tidelity he will ultimately reflect honor on
our ancient Institution." That is the only rule to establish to protect
the Masonic Order and have worthiness in Brothers.
Our Masonic dream should be, stone by stone we rear a sacred
fane, a Temple, neither pa;soda. mosque; no: church; but loftier, simpler,
always open-doored to every breath from Heaven; and truth and peace
and love, and where justice will come and dwell therein.
ln that way we sustain the honor, the glory and the reputation it
has held for ages. Then the practical object of our Institution would
be accomplished, its members living lives of usefulness and virtue.
What more Leautiful teaching does one require than what is set before
our Brother on his initiatory journey? He learns that the Masonic
Order was formed for the practice of brotherly love, relief and truth;
its foundation faith. hope and charity; its supporting pillars temperance, fortitude, prudence and justice.
To debase such gr:md teachings not only dishonor themselves, but
our grand Institution; so every Mason should be more than careful
as to who is admitted.
1t takes a man of worthiness to un<lerstand the subtle, undefinable
influrnce and the sympathy engendere<l by the possession of a common
secret, held sacred and inviolitte. l t prompts to deeds of truest chivalry
and of generous self-sacrifice. This compelling power of Masonry
takes root 111 the heart and comes forth into blossom bearing sweet
odors of charity; peace and happiness <lescend upon him who practices
love and justice.
GEORGE MAIRS PERINE,
Grand Master.

Bro. Chas. L. Patton, for the Masonic Temple Association, reported as follows :
To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
The Directors of the Masonic Temple Association of California
submit the following report:
The Committee to select and recommend a suitable site, after
investigating the advantages of many of the lots offered for the purpose, unanimously reported in favor of a lot on the northwest corner
of Van Ness Avenue and Oak Street, having a frontage of 120 feet on
Van Ness Avenue and also having frontages on Oak Streef and
Hickory Avenue of 109 feet 9 inches.
After investigating the title the Association purchased the property
for the sum of $235,000 and paid for the same out of moneys collected
as follows:
From the Grand Lodge ........................... $195,000.00
From the Grand Chapter . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . 25,000.00
From the Grand Commandery .... . ................ · 15,000.00

$235,000.00
The site is an ideal one, being in the same relative position as to
Market Street as was the old Masonic Temple on Post and Montgomery Streets, and with the expected growth of San Francisco we
may look forward with assurance to our new Temple being directly ·
in the center of the best business portion of San Francisco in the near
future.
The Directors will at once prepare to build the Temple. For this
purpose it will be necessary to select an architect, which should be
done by competition, so that the best result may be obtained, and in
order that we may profit by the work of Masons in other jurisdictions
it will be necessary for us to have the more modern of the Masonic
Temples in the United States visited and examined that we may be
completely up to date.
It will be necessary to raise the necessary funds for the erection
of the Temple from Lodges throughout this jurisdiction.
We propose to proceed actively in all these matters and sincerely
hope and even expect to be ready to lay the corner-stone of our New
Masonic Temple at or before the next session of our Grand Lodge.
The Directors here desire to personally express to R:. w:. Brother
Rueben H. Lloyd, Deputy Grand Master, our appreciation of his great
services in the acquiring of .this site. He has given us the benefit of
his long experience and great knowledge of the value of real estate

59

and also the benefit of his legal experience in clearing away all questions in regard to the title of the property.
. . .
.
We regret that serious illness has kept him from parhc1pat~on. m
the closing of the transaction, but we are glad to hear that he is improving and sincerely hope that his health may be such that he may be
able to act with us in the work remaining to be done.
Respectfully submitted,
By order of the Board of Directors.
FRJ!D L. WIGHT,
CHAS. L. PATTON,
E. P:EABODY,
ORRIN s. HENDJ!RSON,
Committee.

Brother James H. MacLafferty introduced the following resolution:
WH:ER:EAS, There has existed for the past twenty years an organization known as The Masonic Relief Association of the United States
and Canada, whose aim and object it is to facilitate the. disco.very and
exposure of persons traveling about the country and 1mposmg upon
.
.
the charities of Masons; and
WHEREAS This organization has grown in importance, lookmg at
all times to the best charitable interests of the fraternity'. by publ~shing,
in addition to the frauds and impostors, requests for mformahon of
missing brethren, and reporting existence of clandestine bodies, with
their name, number, and location, and
WH:EREAS, The prevailing idea that Lodges are able to pe;~orm the
work of detecting impostors is an erroneous one, as experience and
judgment amply show, because, assuming that Lod~es are very careful
in their disbursement of charity to strange apphcants, the chances
of imposition are many times increased by reason of the fact that
the Lodges applied to have not been forewarned, and
WH:ERJ!AS In case the Grand Lodge of California becomes a subscriber to th~ Masonic Relief Association of the United States and
Canada their warning circulars will be sent to each subordinate Lodge
in the Grand Jurisdiction of California at a cost of said Grand Lodge
of one-half cent per capita per annum on their total membership,

The Grand Lodge is to be congratulated on the efficient corps of
inspectors in the various districts throughout the jurisdiction; they are
all Brethren who not only know· the work, but who are capable of

I wish at this time to extend to the Inspectors and officers and
members of the districts where I have held Schools of Instruction, my
sincere thanks for their attendance and attention and for the courtesies
extended to me during the past year.
The net gain in membership this year has been the greatest in the
history of the Grand Lodge, -and eleven new Lodges have been formed
since our last Communication.
I am indebted to the v:. w:. Geo. Johnson, Past Grand Secretary for the many kindnesses extended to me in his office during the
year.
I° have had the pleasure and company of our M:. w:. Grand
Master, George Mairs Perine, on several of my visits and have
listened to his instructive and interesting gems of Masonic thought, at
the meetings and banquets, and have also had the pleasure and gratification of hearing the M:. w:. Grand Master confer the work and
lecture in the third degree almost letter perfect on several occasions.
I have held several Schools of Instruction in Oakland, Berkeley,
and Alameda, and have given private instruction to Inspectors,
Masters, Wardens, and Deacons in my office here, and have held
Schools of Instruction in many of the Lodges of this city and have
been at all times at the co"mmand of the officers and members of the
Fraternity.

to hold the Schools of Instruction this year commencing Sunday,

night, October 14th, t\-ie third degree will be exemplified by Mill Valley
Lodge, No. 356, of Mill Valle.y ; and on Thursday night the second
degree will be exemplified by Richmond Lodge, No. 375, of this city;
and thus an opportunity will be afforded for the Inspectors, and for
officers of the Lodges to attend the entire sessions of the Grand Lodge
and yet not miss the Schools of Instruction.

The Grand Lecturer presented his Annual Report, as
follows:
To the M:. w:. Grand Lodge of California:
I herewith submit to you my report as Grand Lecturer. During
the past year I have endeavored to reach every district in the State
and have done so, with the execption of the 13th, 4Ist, and 58th,
located respectively in Mono, Inyo, and Imperial counties. I have
held Schools of Instruction in every district, both day and night
sessions, and ii1 most instances the officers and Brethren have attended
the schools and have been eager and anxious to learn the work letter
perfect. Some of the Lodges, located as they are in districts where
the members are scattered, and not having any candidates, have become somewhat rusty in the work; but even In those districts the
Brethren have been in attendance at all the School5 of Instruction to
renew the lectures and floor work. It is certainly a very great pleasure
for me to report to the Grand Lodge and the Brethren the excellent
condition of the Lodges throughout the State.
·
The secretaries are diligent in the collection of dues, and the
manner of conducting the business of the Lodges. The Masters and
Wardens, in most places, have the work almost letter perfect. Much
proficiency has been accomplished since the Wardens have been required to learn the work of the first and second degrees before they
could be installed. It is not only better for the officers themselves, but
better for the Lodges. I can but follow the admonition of my predecessor that the incoming Masters should be extremely careful in their
selection of appointed officers, and only appoint Brethren who will

mittees who examine new members invariably find that the Brothers
know but little of the third degree. The Lodges might make it an
incentive for the candidate to learn the third degree by presenting him
with a Grand Lodge diploma when he has made the necessary proficiency. These diplomas could be gotten up in a smaller form than
the present ones, so that they could be conveniently carried in the
pocket. . I hope that some action will be taken in regard to this matter
by this Grand Lodge, a11d that the custodians of the work be given
power to formulate the lecture.
I regret to report that some of the Secretaries do not comply with
the requirements of the Constitution in reference to sending in their
Grand Lodge reports, some being more than a month overdue. I have
received reports from every Inspe'ctor in. the jurisdiction, except the
24th and 44th, and they all report, as a rule, the Lodges in their several
districts to be doing good work and in a flourishing condition.
I regret that space will not permit the presenting of each report
in full. From my own personal observation, Masonry throughout the
State was never in a more prosperous condition.

W hile the calls for Masonic charity, during the year just past,
have not been so numerous as heretofore, they have been far more
urgent-the individual cases far more appealing- the distress more
keen.
The financial depression throughout the world, has affected the
Brother Mason and his family as well as the business man. I attribute
this depression as one of the chief causes of distress in our household.
Another cause is the transportation of invalid Masons, or members of
their families to the Pacific Coast, in the hope of regaining their
already destr~yed health. This latter is, indeed, an unfortunate mistake.
The Brother simply leaves his home, family and acquaintances, and at
great expense to himself or others comes amo?g ..strangers, on!~ to
pass to the great beyond. This, my Breth ren, 1s worthy of serious
and melancholy reflection."
MASONIC EMPLOYMENT BUREAU.
The Masonic Employment. Bureau continues ~o do good wor~,
finding positions, either great or small, fo r worthy Brothers, appro~1rilately at the rate of one each day. We believe a bureau of hke
C'haracter should be established in all cities of suitable size.

Brother Benj. F. Bledsoe, from the Committee on the
Grand 11aster·s Address, reported as follows:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee to whom was assigned the consideration and
distribution of the reports of the M.'. W.' . Grand Master, the V.'. w:.
Grand Secretary, and the reports referring to the Masonic Home at
Decato, beg leave to report as follows:
We desire to congratulate this Grand Lodge upon the energy,
ability and tmstinted activity displayed by the M.'. w:. Grand Master
during the term of office just closed. The whole report breathes a
spirit of Masonic effort and teems with evidences of Masonic duty
well performed. Diligence, energy, and assiduity seem to have been
the tokens of his tenure of the office.
Special mention, we think, should be made of the fact that during
the past year the greatest net gain in membership in Masonry in California has been made. lt speaks well for the present prosperity and
progress of the Craft, and demonstrates that, though secret fraternal
organizations are multiplying rapidly, Freemasonry still retains its
hold upon, and exacts its allegiance from, those who are desirous of
worshiping at the shrine of fraternal association. We note with satisfaction, from his report, the successful effort to suppress a clandestine
Lodge in San Francisco. Clandestine Masonry, ever a menace to the
interests of our Craft, and a stench in the nostrils of humanity

90

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

·generally, is making an insidious attempt to find a permanent lodgment
in California. Our efforts should be unremitting in its absolute effacement.
The M:. w:. Grand Master in most fitting manner calls attention
to the untimely demise of certain members of our \~raft. We recommend that a special committee of three on Necrology be appointed,
that a suitable and i1tting testimonial of the many virtues of our departed dead may receive adequate consideration.
Twenty decisions, made generally in answer to questions propounded, are reported by the M:. W.". Grand Master. We recommend
that each of these decisions, together with that relating to the question
of the failure of Lodges to elect their officers at the appoined time, be
referred to the Committee on Jurisprudence.
The matter relating to the disapproval of the by-laws of Franklin
Lodge, we recommend should be referred to the Committee on By-Laws.

Philippine Masonry has its origin and carries on its labor under

The Grand Orient of Spain was founded in 1811 by Count de
Grasse Tilly, antl was formally constituted in. Madrid on the 4th
day of July, 1811, by Jonah Drummond, Sovereign Grand Inspec~or­
General of the Northern Jurisdiction of the United States of America,
A. A. S. R.
Sad to say, this Grantl Botly was short-lived, owing to the
brutal absolutism of Ferdinand VII, who, with :fire and sword and
with all the ·pow1Jr and terror of the Inquisition, determin~d to s~p­
press antl destroy the Orcler, and partially succeecling. Still, dnrrng
the years of 1821, 1839, 1844 and 1859 separate attempts were made
to re-establish the Gran<l Loclge.
It was but natural that, owing to the' political conditions of the
country during these reriods, and the iron hand of the Government,

in suppressing the ·Order ancl against the members thereo~, .that many
and various Masoni<J Bodies shoulcl crop up, some legitimate, and

were in ·Spain the following Grand Masonic Bodies:
El Grande Orients Nacional de E spana.
La Confederacion Masonia tlel Congress de Sevilla.
The above bodies were off-shoots antl held their charters by
~irtue o.f the original Constitution of 1811. Besides these, there
existed under the wing and authority of the Grand Lodge of France:
Lodge La Sagesse, a.ml
Lodge La Lib.e rtad.
All of t.hese bodies worketl entirely independent of one another,
and it can be readily seen that this, with regular relations with no

0110 in particular, led to much confusion. Matters went on in this

It was there resolved unanimously by all Representat ives of the

This body progressed somewhat, but owing to the political conditions and dissensions, and such discord within the Grand Body itself,

ond social life, by both Church and Government, but in spite of all

on and live forever.
With this preamble we approach the History of Freemasonry in
the Philip.p ine Islands. Many of the old officials of the Government
who were connected with the Philippine !~lands during their colonial ·
days were members of the Order, and in a quiet way assisted the
same to grow whenever and wherever they could.
Nevertheless the same vicissitudes and disturbances that proved
so detrimental to the growth of the Order in Spain were encountered
in the Philippines, the Church always, and the Government often,
persecuting its votaries. Men were thrown into prison without trial,
aild without charges-simply for being known to be Masons. And
this state of affairs existed to quite recent date, so that the history
of the Order, as it existed before the occupation of this country
by the American Government, is rather a broken series .of happenings of the periods during which it existed or was allowed to rise
and fall by those in power.
Masonry worked. here and there throughout the Islands in secret,
and in ~ome cases without any regular charter or Constitution, ex·
cept the regular number, until during the years of 1886 and 1889 ~
(when some little tolerance was shown), when there were chartered
by the various Grand Bodies existing in Spain, several Lodges. These
worked very quietly and spread the doctrine until the year 1889,
when the Government, owing to the adverse influence brought to
bear agafost the Masonic Bodies in the Philippines by the Church,
treated all members of the Order as political conspirators. They
~ere taken out and shot without trial, thrown into prison without
a hearing, and everything was done by those in power to exterminate the Order completely. 'l'he result was that the working
charters were hidden away, many of the old documents lost and destroyed, and even some of the cbarters were sent out of the country.
This kept up until the war with Spain, when, under ·our liberal
institutions, Spanish"Filipino Masonry has again raised its head
and is at the present time in a flourishing condition. There are
at the present time in existence the following charters in the Phillipine Islands. 'fheir names will indicate their rank and age, being
each in the order in which they are given:

of

In 1893 a Grand Lollge was formed in the Philippine Islands
by the above bodies, with Abrosia Flores, as Grand Master. But it
was very aho1·t-live<l, owing to the acute persecution commenced
against it by the church and state. Its Grand Officers were huntecl
nnd persecuted, antl within a very few months after its inception
most of its officers were either thrown into prison or taken out and
shot.
A crusade was commenced by the local government against its
Order, from 1892 to 1896, which the old members (in speaking of
it to the writer) speak of with horror. No man's life was safe
if he was ever known to have affiliateu or had anything to do with
the principles of Masonry. It was owing to this crusade during these
years that many of th.:i old documents which would have proved of
inestimable historical value were lost. Their history as recited to
the writer could, in many cases, only be authenticated by word of
mouth.
Still, the Spanish-Filipino Masons have shown that they too
like their brethren in Spain, could be true to the Order, even to th~
gjving up of their lives, and in spite of the fact that their Grand

104

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

Master and their Grand Inspectors were shot to death, and others
were deported from the country and imprisoned without trial, they
continued to meet in secret and so thoroughly guarded their charters
that when the time at last came, and they could publicly hold up
their heads, the old Lodges sprang to life immediately, and those
working are now prosperous and gaining in membership right along.
Of the higher Scottish Rite bodies, there are several here working up
to the eighteenth degree, and their influence and teachings to the
Craft and its members are for the best.
There are also in existence a number of Lodges to whom charters have been granted by the Grand Orient of France, which is now
under interdiction. A movement is on foot at the present time to
have the legitimate Grand Lodge of France take these Lodges over.
The membership of the aforementioned Lodges' is composed of good
men, who, of course, are not versed in Masonic law, and supposed
that their charters were granted by a legitimate authority. If the
regular Grand Lodge of France decides favorably on their application, it will a<ld about. 2,000 more members to the roll of those working under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Spain.
This is comparatively a brief resume of the history of Philippine
Masonry to date. It is comparatively new, so to speak. Its future
lies before it. The leaders are men who are trying to carry out the
great principles of fraternal toleration and unity, knowing no race,
creed or color, and it ie to be hoped that under our liberal form of
government they may prosper and grow until such time that will
without doubt come in the future, when they will be brought under
the wing of our American Grand Bodies, and with proper precept
and counsel grow and prosper.
Respectfully 8ubmitted,
(Signed) Lours T. GRANT, Past Master

Brother Murphey, from the same committee, also presented the folowing report:
To the M.". w:. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee, to whom was referred the trial record in the
case of Charles Boxton, expelled by California Lodge, No. l, F. &
A. M., have had the same under consideration and respectfully report
as follows:
The charge contains three specifications, briefly stated as follow s :
1. The accused as a member of the Board of Supervisors of the
City and County of San Francisco, and as a member of the Public
Utility Committee thereof, entered into an immoral agreement and
conspiracy with one T . V. Halsey, whereby accused agreed to assist
said Halsey in attempting by means of bribery to influence the votes
and actions of his fellow members in said Board of Supervisors and
said Public Utility Committee in the matter of the application of the
Home T elephone Company for a franchise, and in furtherance of said
conspiracy and agreement, the accused did assist the said Halsey, etc.

2.

111

That the said accused did receive the said bribe from Halsey

11111111 the understanding that his official vote, opinion, judgment. and
11 tlon

as a member of sail! board and said committee in the matter
franchise should be influenced thereby.
3. The said accused did receive from the said Halsey the sum of
l,000 as a bribe and compensation for his vote and official action as
1 member of the said Board of Supervisors and Public Utility Comlllittce in the matter of said franchise.
The Trial Commissioners foun d against the accused upon each
11( the specifications and also upon the charge of unmasonic conduct,
UHi fixed the penalty of expulsion. The accused appeals upon the
I' I ound that not sufficient legal evidence was introduced to warrant a
1 nnviction, and furthermore that the testimony of the accused given
111 the Superior Court of the City and County of San Francisco in
the case of the People v. Glass, a certified transcript of which testimony
relied upon to support the findings of the Commissioners in this
llllllter, ancl furthermore that said testimony was given under a contrnct of immunity, and was therefore not voluntary and inadmissable;
1111<1 lastly upon the grounds that only a portion of the testimony of the
11ccused offered at said trial was introduced in evidence.
From the testimony of the sho rthand reporter who took the testi11101,y at the t~ial in the Superior Court, it appea rs that all the testinwny was transcribed, and that only the objections, rulings, exceptions
1111cl colloquy, and the cross-examination of the accused by the defend·
11nt's counsel, were omitted. 1f there was anything in the crossrxamination of Boxton that was material it was a matte r of defen se
nncl should have been offered by the accused, who was represented at
the trial by able counsel. The evidence offered was not hearsay, . but
was the solemn admissions of the accused in a court of law, sanctified
by his oath, and when legally proven in a Masonic tribunal conMtituted proper and competent evidence. The fact that the testimony
was given in the State court under a contract of immunity is totally
Immaterial as affecting its admissability at a Masonic trial. A Mason
who publicly and under the solemnity of an oath, in a court of justice,
confesses the commission of grave public offenses, will not be permitted to shield his depravity by a plea that his act was induced by · a
promise of immunity.
Except inferentially, the evidence is not sufficient to sustain the
findings of the Trial Commissioners on the first specification. Upon
the second and third specification the findings of the Trial Commis1ioners are supported by sufficient evidence, a nd we are not disposed
to interfere with their conclusions.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
ndoption :

To the M.". W.". Grdnd Lodge of California:

Your Committee on Grievances, to whom was referred a transcript of the trial of Brother Walter Hubbard of Phrenix Lodge, No.
178, F. & A. M., upon charges preferred against him by Brothers
George S. Pierce and E. L. Aldrich of the same Lodge, submit the
following:
The charge against the accused, in addition to unmasonic conduct,
is in brief that he, as Secretary of said Lodge, embezzled the funds
thereof to the amount of $874.52 between January !st, 1903, and December 1st, 1906.
By order of Past Grand Master Hart the trial thereof was transferred to San Bernardino Lodge, No. 348, F . & A. M. · The transcript
shows that the trial was conducted in due form. The accused admitted
that he had appropriated the money, but strangely enough he was
found not guilty thereof, but guilty of unmasonic conduct. On this
finding he was sentenced to receive a reprimand. In this view of the
matter it is easy to see what parties, if any, are deserving of a reprimand. It ought to be clea r by this time to all Masons that unmasonic
conduct is not a Masonic offense upon the finding of which sentence
can be imposed. The judgment should be reversed and the matter
remanded, with instructions to the trial Lodge to do its plain duty in
the premises. Your committee so advises.

Sec. 429 Anderson's Manual.
Sec. 388 Anderson's Manual.
It has been held repeatedly that embezzlement is a Masonic offense.
The law of our fraternity is that when a Mason commits an offense
which is a violation of the moral law and of the law of the land, he
abo commits a Masonic crime, because he thereby brings shame upon
the Craft.
Sec. 140 Anderson's Manual.
The crime of embezzlement is one of the greatest. Masonry seeks
In attain a higher object than that of glossing over the misdeeds of its
nicmbers, and should make no distinction among its members.
Sec. 254 Anderson's Manual.
The fact that the Brother pleaded not to be expelled or confessed
hb errors and expressed sorrow for his faults and asks to be forgiven
IM not sufficient. If it were, every unworthy Mason who has been
expelled could be restored, and Masonic pu·nishment would be a byword
11ml a reproach.
Sec. 157 Anderson's Manual.
The law ot our Order prohibits a Lodge from receiving a petition
from a person under indictment by a Grand Jury.

Hence there should be no question that when a Mason has been
convicted and sentenced to serve a "term in · state's prison, he is no
longer entitled to the protection of Masonry.
'there may be some insta11ces in which such would be the case,
but not in this class of crimes.
The Trial Commissioners in this case seem to have gone in the
highways and byways looking for all kinds of rumors. They say in
their report :
"From its first organization this Commission realized the serious
nature of the duty imposed upon it," and "we believe a Masonic Trial
Commission to be in some respects less and in other respects more
than a mere judicial machine," held it to be their duty to avail themselves of any and all evidence from whatever source obtainable that
might throw light upon the acts and motives of the accused in the
premises. While realizing the non-value oi hearsay evidence as affect..
ing a conviction, ·we believe it to be a Masonic as well as a civic duty
t.q take cognizance of such facts as we of our own knowledge find to
·exist. He (Lovelace) chose rather to plead guilty than to actively
defend himself, knowing that such defense would expose, disgrace
and possibly involve more seriously members of this fraternity which
he dearly loved."
This trial commission has violated many rules of our Masonic
law pertaining to trials.
The rule is that testimony must be taken in full by question and
.
answer, tie reduced to writing and signed by the witness.
Sec. 668 and 687, Anderson's Manual.
The evidence upon which _the Commissioners acted must be sent
up.
Sec. 187, Anderson's Manual.
"All oral testimony, direct and cross, will be written out in full
py the Secretary."
Sec. 14, Forms for Record of Trials.
The . Commissioners have no right to hear testimony except when
assembled, and both the accused and accuser being pr~sent if they so
desire; also the Master and Secretary. The latter must record all
testimony given and transmit a copy thereof to this Grand Lodge.
,, It follows that this Commission comes clearly within the rule :
"In a clear case, when_ the facts are admitted and the law is plain,
only one verdict could honestly be reached, and it might well be said
that Commissioners who should, in disregard of the duty they owed
to themselves, their Lodge and the great body of Masons, render a
verdict of acquittal in such a case, were no longer worthy to wear the
badge of a Mason ; charges might properly be preferred against them,

for by their perfidy they had shown themselves deserving the severest
penalty known to our laws."
Sec. 265, Anderson's Manual.

Involved in this crime with the Brother in question, that their names
1hould be ascertained and dealt with in a like manner.

adoption.

ac~uitting Brother Charles E. Lovelace be, and the same is hereby, set
aside, and that Brother Charles E. Lovelace be and he is hereby expelled from all of the rights and privileges of Masonry.

M. '. W .'. Frank M. Angellotti, chairman ·of the Committee on Jurisprudence, presented the following reports:
To the M. '. W.' . Grand Lodge of California:
We have had under consideration the decisions of the Grand
Master on questions of Masonic law, as stated in his address, and
report thereon as follows :
1. The first is one relative to the right of a subordinate Lodge
to receive by affiliation one having no <limit, but holding papers showing
that he had been a member of Lodge El Porvenir, No. 2, in Madrid and
the Grand Orient of Spain, both of which had gone out of existence
in the year 1891. The law was correctly stated by the Grand Master
on both points decided, viz. : first, that the inability of an applicant
for affiliation to procure a <limit from the jurisdiction of which he has
ceased to be a member will not stand in the way of affiliation where a
satisfactory explanation in writing of the inability to furnish the same
is made; and, second, that no one can be recognized as a Mason and
received by affiliation, unless he has regularly been made a Mason in
some Lodge acting under a charter or dispensation from a Grand
Lodge recognized by us as possessing proper Masonic standing and
authority to grant such a charter or dispensation. We recommend that
the decision be approved.

118

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

2. The action of the Grand Master in designating other Lodges
for the trial of various cases where it was made to appear that the
Master of the Lodge where the charges were pending, or the Lodge
itself, was disqualified to conduct a trial, or that the convenience of
witnesses made such a change expedient; was in accord with our law.
This covers the second, fourth, fifth, sixth, and ninth rulings of the
Grand Master as stated in his address, and we recommend that the
same be approved.
3. In two other cases reported in the seventh and tenth rulings,
it appearing to the Grand Master that the Master of the Lodge in
which the charges were pending would be a witness at the trial, he
did not transfer the case, but designated the Master of another Lodge
to preside at the trial. This course has, heretofore, been approved by
the Grand Lodge in at least. two instances (Vol. 11, Pro. p. 587; Vol.
13, Proc. p. 180). So far as cases in which the Master is disqualified
simply by reason of the fact that he is a material witness on one side
or the other are concerned, these rulings have never been expressly overruled; but it has always been the law of this jurisdiction, that where
the Master is the accuser, directly or indirectly, as where he directs the
prosecution of the charges by the Junior Warden, or is the injured
party in the matter of the accusation, not only is he disqualified to
preside, but his Lodge is disqualified to try the case, and it must be
transferred to some other Lodge for trial. 11 Proc. 587, 17 Proc. 247,
24 Proc. 645.)
We find no authority in our constitution or regulations for the
designation of a Master to preside at a trial in any other Lodge than
his own, and consider it the better and safer course under our laws
as they now exist to transfer the case to another Lodge for trial
whenever the Master is disqualified to preside for any cause.
It might be advisable to so amend our law that where the disqualification is purely personal to the Master, and does not affect the
Lodge, the Senior Warden may preside in place of the Master, and
if he also be disqualified, then the Junior Warden. It may be suggested that the Master should not be held disqualified for the mere
reason that he is to be a witness, unless he is to be a material witness
on the question of the guilt or innocence of the accused.
The decisions of the Grand Master in these two cases being m
accord with the previous decisions, we recommend that the same be
approved.
4. The eighth ruling was to the effect that any Lodge in the
City and County of San Francisco has jurisdiction to entertain and
try charges of unmasonic conduct against a Mason residing in said
city and county, but who is a member of a Lodge outside thereof.
This was in accord with our law (Sec. 1, Art. IV, Part 6, Con.),
and we recommend its approval.

ul 1pted a few years ago, a non-affiliated Mason who has neglected to

M.'. W.'. Frank M. Angellotti, chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows: .
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Following is the "Address to the Great Fraternity of Free and
Accepted Masons of the United States of America, through their
representatives in Grand Lodge assembled," emanating from the Grand
Lodge of Tennessee, and referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence :
The Grand Lodge of the Ancient and Honorable Fraternity of
Free and Accepted Masons of the State of Tennessee, believing the use
of cipher rituals of the Symbolic Degrees of Masonry to be un-Masonic,
illegal and fraught with danger to Freemasonry, has, by edict, forbidden

LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

121

their purchase, sale. or use within its jurisdiction, and has. al~ invited
It• sister Grand Lodges to unite with it in a resolute· purpose to suppress this baleful and un-Masonic practice, and it rejoices in the
favorable . responses thereto received from the great majority of the
American Grand Jurisdictions; but this Grand Body has heard with
regret and astonishment that some Grand Lodges of the United States
not only do not forbid, but, on the contrary, expressly authorize the
use of printed rituals, purporting to describe the secret work of the
Symbolic Degrees, and even print and furnish copies thereof to their
1ubordinates, whereby the hidden mysteries of Freemasonry may be
unlawfully divulged.
Some publish specious arguments in excuse for so doing, as did
the Grand Orient of France for its action in removing the Bible from
Its altars. Such conduct and action in the one case as in the other,
IA wholly repugnant to the work and genius of the Freemasonry of
Tennessee, as we have received it from the fathers, and are bound to
transmit it to posterity. It is a plain breach of obligation and duty in
letter and spirit, and a course not open for argument. Our fraternal
relation to these grand bodies, however, suggests that possibly such
contrary views and practices may sp~ing from differ.ent systems of
Freemasonry, built upon different foundations, having different rituals
nnd obligations, and not of the same origin, faith or practice. Surely
their ways are not our ways and their landmarks cannot be ours.
In view of this, and that no cause of misunderstanding or complaint
may exist against the Grand Lodge of Tennessee for any course it may
he compelled to pursue, this Grand Lodge hereby declares its abiding
faith in, and unswerving loyalty to, the following fundamental tenets
of Freemasonry, received, maintained and cherished as we have ever
learned and taught, by all Free and Accepted Masons always and everywhere:
1. Freemasonry has as essentials certain secrets of ritual·
which it forever conceals and never reveals to any person in the
world except its own members.
2. These ancient mysteries are communicated only by the instructive tongue to the attentive ear and are safely lodged in the
faithful breast; and any other mode of communication in Ancient
Craft Masonry is most positively forbidden in solemn form and
manner.
3. So likewise is forbidden the writing, printing or marking
in any manner, of these secrets or any sign or letter thereof,
whereby the same becomes legible or intelligble to any person, lest
these secrets might become known to the profane.
4. No individual Mason is exempt from the obligation of profound secrecy, and no- human power can authorize him to write,
print or mark Masonic secrets in any manner whatsoever.

122

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

GRAND LODGE OF CALIFORNIA

5. These secrets are ancient landmarks of Freemasonry and
no body of men, inside or outside of Lodge or Grand Lodge, has
power to make innovations in Ancient Craft Masonry.
Standing upon these ancient precepts of our brotherhood, we are
not at liberty to violate them, nor to encourage or sanction their violation by others of our fraternity and obligation. We must obey them,
and. so must all within the sacred precincts; and the inevitable consequences of disobedience must rest upon those who will not obey. It
is no excuse or justification for any, that men are eager to break these
laws, or that men have broken them before, or that in other degrees or
orders of American Masonry cipher rituals may be in common use.
Our duty and obligation, as Ancient Craft Masons, compel our
obedience to these ancient regulations.
In Tennessee we are resolved to remain true to our vows, steadfast
to our trust, and not to abjure the faith nor suffer innovations in our
work. And we earnestly and fraternally call upon all our brother
Masons of the Ancient York Rite, now happily the American Rite of
Symbolic Masonry, wherever they may reside, to abide with us in our
unalterable purpose and resolve to preserve the landmarks and keep
sacred and inviolate the secrets of our beloved fraternity. Hitherto
we have all been of one mind in this course, and all has gone well
with us. The restless spirit of change ,and modern habits of impatience
are bringing disorder and confusion into our counsels, and unless
resisted and routed will, by innovation, bring discord to our own
ranks and destruction to our peace and harmony. Let us all stand
together in the ancient ways.
For the Committee of Jurisprudence,
H ENRY H . INGERSOLL, Secretary.

T ennessee, as expressed in the fo regoing address, and recommend its
approval by the Grand Lodge.

To the M.". w:. Grood Lodge of California:

THOS. FLfNT,

The question whether a Lodge under dispensation has the power
under our Constitution to entertain and try charges of un-Masonic
conduct has been suggested. The Grand Master was asked to give his
opinion thereon, but as it was discovered that there was no actual case
involving the question demanding a decision ; no opinion was
given. The matter was, however, referred by him to this committee,
as it was recognized that the matter was one as to which the law should
be clear. After a careful investigation of the written law and decisions
of this Grand Lodge, we have come to the conclusion that a Lodge
under dispensation has such power. While it is clear that the Master
of such a Lodge should have the jurisdiction to receive charges of
misconduct (for otherwise our law is so written that there would be
no way of presenting charges against a Mason who is a member of
such a Lodge and who resided within its jurisdiction where no other
Lodge has concurrent jurisdiction over the same territo~y), we feel
that there are ver' serious objections to allowing such a Lodge to
conduct trials for Masonic offenses and to pronounce judgments of ..
suspension or expulsion. W e believe, therefore, that the Constitution
should be amended in such a way as to provide that while proceedings
for un-Masonic conduct may be instituted by the presentation of the
charges to the Master of such a Lodge, where the accused is a member
thereof, or resides within its exclusive territorial jurisdiction, but
that when charges are so instituted the Grand Master shall designate
some chartered Lodge for the trial thereof.

SAMUEL
DENSON,
CHARLES L. PATTON,

M." . \V:. Charles L. Patton, from the Committee
cm J urlsprudence, presented the following:
To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
The Grand Master decided that a Tyler could be appointed who· is
not a member of the Lodge. It has been a custom to appoint a Tyler
to act for two or more Lodges where they all meet in the same hall.
The constitutional provisions in relation to officers elected and appointed
11re to be found in P art IV, Art. I, Constitution.
Section 1 directs that the Master, Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary shall be elected annually at the stated meeting preceding the
nnniversary of St. John the Evangelist.
Section 2 provides how elections may be held, if not had at the
stated meeting prescribed.
Section 4 prescribes that the Deacons, Tyler and such other subordinate officers as the By-Laws of the Lodge may designate, shall be
appointed in such manner as the By-Laws may direct.
The uniform Code of By-Laws provides in Article II that the
Master, Senior and Junior Wardens, Treasurer and Secretary shall
be elected by ballot, and that the other officers shall be appointed.

126

PROCEEDINGS OF THE

It. is only in Section 3, of Article I, Part IV, of the Constitution
that any attempt is made to fix any qualification for office, either
elective or appointive. This section prescribes that none but members
in good standing, whose dues are paid, shall be entitled to vote at an
election, and that any voter shall be eligible to any office in the Lodge.
The only decision on the subject seems to be No. 877, "Anderson's
Manual," which is to the effect that under the provisions of our Constitution and Code of By-Laws a Brother who is in arrears for dues
at the time of the annual election, and who has been granted an extension, is ineligible to office in the Lodge.
Part IV, Article I, Section 3, of the Constitution, in one view of
it supports the Grand Master's ruling. It might be construed, and we
think it should be construed, on the principle that the enumeration of
persons who can hold office in the Lod.ge excludes all others from
office holding ;•this, however, is not as clear as it might be, and we
think the Grand Master might well construe the Constitutional provision as he· did.
We believe that it is the meaning of the con·stitutional provision
that the officers should all be members of the Lodge, and we so construe it.
We also believe that the best interests of a Lodge require care in
the selection of a Tyler, and that frequently where two or more Lodges
meet in the same hall a better Tyler can be secured by appointing the
same Brother to act for each of the Lodges, and think that it would
be wise to make it clear that a Tyler could be appointed in such a case
to act for both Lodges.
We therefore offer the following resolution and recommend its
adoption:
Resolved, That Section I of Article II of the Uniform Code of
By-Laws be amended by adding thereto the followfig:
"Any Master Mason in good standing, whether or not a member of
the Lodge, may be appointed Tyler."

Which was adopted.

Brother Benjamin F. Bledsoe, Chairman of the Committee on Charters, submitted the following report:
To the M. ·. w. ·. Grand Lodge of California:

We, your Committee on Charters, beg leave t-:> report as follows:
During the past year dispensations ha\'.e been regularly issued and
granted to the following named Lodges, viz.:
Imperial Lodge . .......... .... . Nov. 1, 1907.
East Belt Lodge ..... . . . .. .. . . . Nov . 12, 1907.
West Lake Lodge . .......... . .. Dec. 10, 1907.
Balder Lodge . .......... .. ..... Mch. 12, 1908.
University Lodge .............. Mch. 27, 1908.
Turlock Lodge ... .... . .... .. ... . May 28, 1908.
Apollo Lodge ................ .. May 29, 1908.
Rising Light Lodge ... . .. ... ... . May 29, 1908.
Fowler Lodge ........ .. ........ June 2, 1908.
Fraternity Lodge .............. June 15, 1908.
Burlingame Lodge .. : .......... July 8, 1908.
All of these Lodges above named have applied for charters. We
have carefully examined all their proceedings, papers, books and
records, and fin<l that in the main they comply with and conform to
the requirements of the Constitution and General Regulations of this
Grand Lodge.
We note, with a very emphatic degree of di~favor, a disposition
on the part of some of the Lodges whose records were before us, to
fail to follow the form of a record provided for "Example Lodge" and
to be found in Anderson's Manual. There can be no sufficient excuse
for this. Therein is provided in fullest detail, a form for the record
to be kept by the Secretary of a Lodge, particularly a Lodge starting
upon its Masonic career, and for the sake not only of uniformity but
also of correctness and completeness of detail, every Secretary in
engrossing his minutes should consider it his especial duty to conform
thereto. If such is <lone a clearer, neater and more comprehensive
record will be secured, matters of importance will not be' omitted and
the labors of the Committee on Charters will be measurably lessened.
In this connection, by way of contrast, and in order that commendation may be awarded where commendation is unquestionably due,
we desire to call the attention of the members of this Grand Lodge to
the records of Balder Lodge, U . D., of this city. They are perfect
in form, appearance an<l substance, and reflect unusual and deserved
credit upon the Lo<lge an<l its Secretary.
W e recommend that· charters be granted to each of the abovementioned Lodges, name<l as follows :

DOARD OF RELlEF.

1,000 to the Board of Relief of Oakland.
200 to the Board of Relief of Stockton.

the same varying all the way from five to eight cents per month. We,
therefore, offer the following resolution and recommend its adoption:
Resolved That from and after the date of this Grand Lodge Comnmnication ~o funds of this Grand Lodge shall be appropriated for
Boards of Relief unless they first show satisfactory evidence that they
huvc received the sum of eight cents a month per capita from the
I,•lllges constituting their respective compacts.
