MASONIC RELIEF ASSOCIATION OF THE UNITED STATES AND CANADA.
Your Committee have had under consideration the resolution,
referred to it directing this Grand Lodge to become a subscriber to the
"Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada." We
believe that the money spent in affiliating with this Association will be
the means of saving much larger sums .to this Grand Lodge and to all
the L odges of our jurisdiction, and we offer the following resolution
and recommend its adoption:

Resolved, That this Grand Lodge become a subscriber to the
"Masonic Relief Association of the United States and Canada," and
that the sum of $193.50 be and the same is hereby appropriated from
the funds of this Grand Lodge to pay for said subscription.
REQUEST 01' ROBERT PATTON CHAPTER, UNITED DAUGHTERS OF THE CONFEDERACY.
Your Committee have considered the request of Robert Patton
Chapter, United Daughters of the Confederacy, for A contribution to a
fund for the erection of a statue dedicated to the American soldiers·
who died in the stockade prison on J ohnson's Island, Ohio, and we
are unanimous in praising the efforts being made to honor the memory
of their heroic dead. We feel, however, that the appropriation of Grand
Lodge fund s for purposes not under the control of Masonry will
establish a dangerous precedent likely to cause much trouble hereafter. For this reason we do not feel justified in recommending an
appropriation, and recommend that the request be denied.
CLAIMS OF VARIOUS LODGES.
Your Committee to whom were referred the petition of ·Clear
Lake Lodge, No. 183, Yolo Lodge, No. 81, Gravel Range Lodge, No.
59, and Keystone Lodge, No. 161, asking for the remission of their
Grand Lodge dues for the year, have considered the same, and we find
as follows:
1. That Clear Lake Lodge has a depleted treasury, and two
indigent Brethren to care for, one of them a Brother who was Tyler
of the Lodge for twenty-nine years.
2d. That Yolo Lodge has spent all of its funds in the erection of
a new hall upon the site of a former one which was destroyed by

h11 niture.
3d. That Gravel Range Lodge, No. 59, lost its hall, furniture and
1111111phernalia by fire, and has no insurance thereon.
4th. That Keystone Lodge, No. 161, had its hall badly damaged
111 ~terms and floods, the repair thereof having depleted its treasury,
i11ul placed an indebtedness upon the Lodge of $700.00.
For these reasons your Committee hereby recommends the adoption of the following resolution :
Resolved, That the Grand Lodge dues of Clear Lake Lodge, No.
111.1, Yolo Lodge, No. 81, Gravel Range Lodge, No. 59, and Keystone
I ·><lge, No. 161, for this year, be and the same are hereby remitted.

To the M.'.

w:·. Grand Lodge of California :

Your Committee to whom was referred the trial records in the
case of A. Cazeaux of Vallee de France Lodge, No. 329, and sen- ·
tenced to reprimand by Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42, for unmasonic
conduct, upon charges preferred by the Junior Warden of his own
Lodge, and from which judgment Leon Curtet, the Master of Vallee
de France Lodge at the time the charges were preferred, has appealed,
have had the same under consideration and report as follows:
.
'I'he charge contains two specifications, which set out in effect
that the accused did three times absolutely refuse to obey the gavel
in the hands of the Master; the second specification being in the
nature of an amplification of the first.
The trial was regularly and fairly conducted by . a Trial Commission in a Lodge designated by the Grand Master. The Commissioners found the accused guilty on the first specification and not
guilty as to the second, and fixed reprimand as the penalty.
The appeal is taken upon the sole ground that the punishment
is not commensurate with the gravity of the offense.
.We have carefully examined the record and are impressed with
the manifest spirit of fairness that prevailed at the trial, and upon
the record as presented are not disposed to interfere with the conclusions of the Commissioners.
The accused is a man well advanced in years, has been a member
of the Lodge for eighteen years, and of that time was its Master for
four years, during which latter period he attended every meeting. It
appears that he was of an excitable disposition, characteristic of his
nativity, and that he had an exaggerated opinion of his prerogatives
as a Past Master. In the heat of debate he no doubt transgressed the
rules of proper conduct in the Lodge, and we think merited the punishment awarded by the Commissioners. Further than this we are
unwilling to go on the record presented.
·
We are not unmindful of the gravity of th~ offenses charged,
but in this class of cases no general rule can be laid down, and the
circumstances attending the particular case must govern.
We the refo re offer the following resolution and recornmend. its
adoption :
R esolved, That the action of Los Angeles Lodge, No. 42, sentencing Brother A. Cazeau to reprimand, be and the same hereby is
affirmed.
J. D. MURPHJ;:Y,
Gi;:o. E. CHURCH,

H. M. Owi;:Ns,

'Ne believe that pending such reorganization and adjustment a~
the Special Committee shall pre5ent fer consideration to this Grand
Body, that there are no good reasons for ' making any material improvements and additions to the Home; furthermore, we believe that
$30,000 per annum should pay the operating expenses of said Home.
Therefore recommend that for the coming year the per .capita tax
be placed at 75 cents instead of . $1, which would produce approximately $31,000 for the support of the Home.

M.". W.". Frank M. Angellotti, Chairman of the Committee on Jurisprudence, reported as follows:

the names of the brethren appointed on such Committees be announced

166

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California :

Brother H. ]. Owen has introduced a proposed resolution looking
to a change in our existing law relative to Committees on Investigation. The effect thereof; if adopted, will be to repeal that portion pf
the law enacted by this Grand Lodge in 1907 (Proc. 1907, p. 713),
providing that the names of the Committee shall not be given by the
Master to the Secretary, but that the Master shall himself notify the
members of the Committee of their appointment, not revealing to one
the identity of the other, that the reports of the members of the Committee shall be rendered directly to the Master, and when practicable
given orally, and if in writing that said reports shall be destroyed by
the Master, and that the simple announcement by the Master to the
Lodge of the result shall be all the information concerning those
. reports conveyed by him to anyone. This would leave the law as it
was prior to 1906, supplemented by the resolution adopted that year,
(Proc. 19C-6, p. 464) providing that such reports shall not be read in
the Lodge so far as the announcement of the character of the report
is concerned, and that the names of the brethren appointed on such
Committee shall not be announced in the Lodge.
We see no objection to the proposed resolution of Brother Owe.n,
if it be deemed advisable to return to the old method. Whether we
shall do so or not appears to us, however, to be so purely a question
of policy, and the whole matter has been so recently considered by the
Grand Lodge, that we prefer to leave it for decision without recommendation on our part. We therefore refer the proposed resolutioh to
the Grand Lodge for such action as it deems proper.
The resolution is as follows :
Resolved, That the recommendation in the address of the Grand
Master relative to Committees of Investigation, to be found in the,
report of the Committee on Jurisprudence on page 713 of Proceed-ings of 1907, is hereby rescinded, and that the resolution relative to
Committees of Investigation adopted at the Fifty-seventh Annual Communication of this M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge, held October 9th to
October 12th, 1906, to be found on page 464 of Proceedings, is hereby
restored, and reading as follows :

"That the reports of Committees of Investigation appointed on the
petition of applicants for the degrees of Masonry, or for applications
for membership, shall not be read in the Lodges, except so far as the
announcement of the character of the report is concerned; nor shall

111 the Lodge."

FRANK M. ANGELLOTTI,
WM. S. WELLS,
Taos. FLINT,
SAMUEL C. DENSON,
CHARLES L. PATTON,
Committee.

n<lopted.

To the M.'. w:. Grand Lodge of California:

The foll owing was submitted by Brother George W . Myers and
referred to this Committee:
WHEREAS: The Clandestine Lodges in this State are trying to
induce regular Masons to visit their Lodges; and
WHEREAS: Many regular Masons do not know what Lodges are
clandestine, and that such Brothers are subject to an examination as
to their knowledge of the secret work of the Order, with no recourse
us to the proof that they are so entitled to receive it.
And believing that safeguards should be provided to protect all
regular Masons; be it
Resolved: That all Lodges in this jurisdiction be required to show
a visiting Brother, on demand, the charter of said Loclge before subjecting him to an examination.
We recommend the adoption of the within resolution.

Report and resolution adopted.

The following was submitted by Brother John T. Morrison and
referred to your Committee on Jurisprudence:

FRANK M. ANGJiLLOTTI,

"Resolved, That the Grand Lecturer be authorized and directed to
formulate and promulgate a suitable catechism for the third degree,
and that each and every Master Mason made subsequent to the adoption of this resolution be required to pass a satisfactory examination
in open Lodge in said catechism befoi;e he shall be entitled to a certificate for a Grand Lodge diploma; and further
"Resolved, That whenever any such Grand Lodge diploma shall be
issued to any Master Mason so certified, it shall be as a reward and
without cost to the Brother receiving it."
·
We do not see that the object sought to be accomplished will be
attained by the proposed resolution. We are further of the opinion
that certain amendment s to our constitution are essential before .a
Brother can be denied a Grand Lodge diploma for failure to qualify
himself in the work of the third degree. We recommend that the
resolution b~ not adopted.
0

The recommendation was adopted and the resolution
did not prevail.
"Resolved, That section 1 of Article IX of the Uniform Code of
By-Laws be and is hereby amended by eliminating the figures $200.00
and substituting the figures $150.00."
The foregoing presents what is purely a question of policy. The.
only suggestion we have to make in the matter is that we should not
make any change in the minimum amount to be paid for life membership, unless we are thoroughly satisfied that such amount will produce
for the Lodge a sufficient revenue so far as the particular member is
concerned. We report it back for such action as the Grand Lodge
deems advisable.

The resolution was adopted.
"Resolved, That electioneering for office in this Grand ·Lodge is
prohibited. Any member guilty of such offense shall be ineligible to
office; and if an officer, shall forfeit the office held by him. The same
rule shall apply in Subordinate Lodges."
We are in full sympathy with the general spirit of this resolution.
We feel, however, that it is not sufficiently definite and certain in its
terms to be enacted as a law. The word "electioneering" is a word
that may be very broadly construed, so construed as to include what is
only legitimate argument on the part of worthy brethren in favor of
the election to some office of the person deemed by them to be the

That Subdivision V of Section I of Article IV of Part II be
amended to read as follows :
5th. '"l'o report, at each Annual Communication, a detailed account
of all moneys received by him during the year, with a specific statement
of the sources whence they were derived, presenting therewith the receipts of the Grand Treasurer therefor; and also a detailed and itemized account of the disbursements of the Grand Lodge during the
year."
That Section 1 of Article IV of Part VI of the Constitution be
amended by adding the following:
"Such charges shall never be presented to the Master of a Lodge
under dispensation if there is a chartered Lodge having concurrent
jurisdiction, over the same territory, except where the accused is a
member of such Lodge under dispensation ; but where the accused is a
member of such a Lodge, . or under or within its jurisdiction, and no
chartered Lodge has concurrent jurisdiction over the same territory,
they may be so presented. When the Lodge to the Master of which
such charges are presented is a Lodge under dispensation, such Master
shall at once transmit the same to the Grand 'Master, who shall thereupon, if it shall appear to him that the act or acts complained of therein
constitute a Masonic offense, designate some chartered Lodge to try
the same, and transmit such charges to the Master thereof, who shall
thereupon proceed therewith in the same manner as if the charges had
originally been presented to him.
BY-LAWS.
That Section. 1 of Article II of the Uniform Code of By-Laws be
amended by adding thereto the following :
Any Master Mason in good standing, whether or not a member of
the Lodge, may be appointed Tyler.
That Section 1 of Article IX of the Unifo rm Code of By-Laws be
and is hereby amended by eliminating the figures $200.00 and substituting therefor the figures $150.00.

Resolved, That the resolution relative to Committee of Investigation, adopted 1906 (page 464, Proc. 1906) is hereby restored, and read~ u~~:

191

I

"That the reports of Committees of Investigation appointed on the
petitions of applicants for the degrees of Masonry, or for applications
for· membership, shall not be read in the Lodge, except so far as the
announcement of the character of the report is concerned; nor shall
the names of the brethren appointed on such Committees be announced
in the Lodge.

Resolved, That the resolution heretofore adopted by the Grand
Lodge that the Report of the Committee on Correspondence be -restricted to fifty pages, be and it is hereby rescinded.
Resolved, That from and after the date of this Grand Lodge Communication, no funds of this Grand Lodge shall be appropriated for
Boards of Relief unless they first show satisfactorily that they have
received the sum of eight cents a month per capita from the Lodges
constituting their respective compacts.
·
Resolved, That the Grand Secretary be instructed to send one copy
of Anderson's Revised Manual to each Lodge in the jurisdiction, to
remain the property of the Lodge, and one copy to each Inspector,· to
be retained by him.
Resolved, That all Lodges in this jurisdiction be required to show
a visiting Brother, on demand, the charter of the Lodge before subjecting him to an examination.
Resolved, 'l'hat the Grand Secretary prepare a uniform receipt for

REPORT
OF

COMMITTEE ON CORRESPONDENCE
OCTOBER, 1908

To the M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge of California:
Your Committee on Correspondence respectfully submits this
n·port:
The M.'. W.'. Grand Lodge at the Communication of 1905 (see
page 147, Proceedings of 1905) adopt;d the following resolution:
"That the Committee on Correspondence limit the extent of its
report so that the same shall not exceed fifty pages, _and that t~e
Name be confined to a digest of facts concerning othe.r jurisdictions,
which may be of special interest to California Masons."
There was no report made by the Committee on Correspondence
11t the last Communication; · this report, therefore, covers the pro'ccedings of Grand Lodges of other jurisdictions for two years. It
might therefore be assumed that its limit should be one hundred pages.
The proceedings · received contain volumes of matter interesting to
Masons. Only a sm~ll part can be presented in this report. Th"e
net of selecting from this great mass, consisting of many thousand
pages, that believed to be most entertaining to California Masons is
n matter of judgment. That which would most interest one, would
not interest another. The effort has been to select for this report
matters which it was thought would most interest the greatest number.
A larger amount of matter has been taken from some Proceedings
than from others, but the same fraternal feeling exists equally toward
nil Masons everywhere. If the Proceedings of any jurisdiction seem
to have been noticed more than another, it has resulted from the
effort to comply with the resolution before quoted.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

A communication is printed from the Grand Secretary of the
Grand Lodge of Washington, D. C., recommending a card certificate
to be given to Master Masons. The Grand Master says: "Many of
our sister Grand Jurisdictions require that a visitor shall produce
a Grand Lodge diploma before he will be admitted." And he thereupon recommends the adoption of a system of card receipts. The
Grand Master recommended that the card certificate should "give such
a description of the member as would identify him and prevent any
who might accidentally or otherwise get possession of the card from
making use of it."
The Committee on Jurisprudence recommended that no action be
had in relation to Card Receipts or Certificates. We quote from
their report as follows : "The possession of a 'Card Receipt' would
not be a guarantee that the brother holding it was not suspended or
expelled, nor would a Grand Secretary's certificate on the back be
evidence that the Charter had not been arrested. The desire for
these changes in old customs and methods, no doubt, arises because
members see things, used by other societies and, therefore, think that
Masonry is not up with the 'spirit of the times' unless She adopts each
new-fangled invention. It may be that in this case the desire of
a printer for new business is responsible. There is nothing in our
Constitution or By-laws to prevent a Lodge from issuing a card or any
other form of receipt it sees proper to use." The Committee further
state that provision is made for the issuance of a diploma by the
Grand Secretary, and that this is documentary evidence which any
Grand Lodge, or its constituent Lodges, would not reject. Continuing
the Committee say : "To rule otherwise would be to say that one
Grand Lodge could legislate for another, or that a member from
Arizona would have to carry a variety of receipts suiting the whim
or fancy of each Grand Lodge he might wish to visit."
The Grand Master recommends that the subject of dimitted Masons
be looked into by the proper committee, and refers to the fact that ,
Masons with <limits, however unworthy, may maintain their Masonic
standing by applying for admission and paying a certain amount of
dues, although their petition is rejected.
In regard to dimitted Masons, the question arises, which perhaps
is easily answered, is it the duty of a Lodge, within whose jurisdiction
a foreign dimitted Mason dies or is sick, to bury or care for him.
Must the Grand Lodge bear such expense, or the local Lodge?
The Constitution of the Grand Lodge of Arizona requires a twothirds vote to reinstate a member who has been suspend~d for nonpayment of dues.
There is no report on correspondence.
Dr. J. Roskruge (Tucson), G. Sec.

ARIZONA.
Twenty-sixth Communication, Morenci, November 19, 1907.
Number of Lodges, 19.

Number of Members, 1,535.
Gain, 141.
Herbert Brown G. M.

The Communication of this Grand Lodge was held in the "stope"
of the Lone Star Mine under the Town of Morenci, and a picture
o~ the Grand Lodge is given as a frontispiece to the Proceedings. The
picture shows the letter "G" suspended on the rocky wall of the stope. ·
A resolution was adopted in which it was stated that the Grand
Lodge .had adopted t~1e principle that each Grand Lodge, as well as its
subordmak Lodges, 1s responsible for the indigent of its Jurisdiction
and that this Jurisdiction holds it to be good Masonic law that whe~
a subordinate Lodge is unable to care for its needy, the Grand' Lodge
should supply the required relief.
It was decided that, when a Lodge or a sister Jurisdiction conferred
a .degree at the request ~f a Lodge of Arizona, "it is entirely optional
with the Lodge conferrmg the degree whether they demand a fee
or not; but, it being an act of Masonic courtesy, we hardly think
that to demand a fee would be exactly the right thing, but believe
that each Lodge should be the sole judge whet'her any fee should be
exacted or not."
The following resolution was adopted:

Resolved, That this Grand Lodge, in regular Communication
assembled, adopt a Standard Ritual of Work in the several degrees
1
for this Territory; that the same be made of record reduced to cipher
published in that form and a copy furnished the Master Senior and
Junior Warden of each Lodge in this Jurisdiction in o;der that the
uniformity that should exist throughout this Territory may be maintained."
The General Regulations are printed in the Proceedings. To
print General Regulations in Grand Lodge Proceedings occasionally
is a commendable procedure. The knowledge of the General Regulations of other Grand Jurisdictions would give an opportunity to make
desired amendments or adopt regulations in use in other Grand Jurisdictions, thus tending to uniformity and harmony.
Regulation No. 4 is as follows: "Resolved: That the Ritual
of the 'Grand Lodge of California' be, and it is hereby adopted as the
Standard Work or Ritual of the Most Worshipful Grand Lodge of
the Territory of Arizona."

8

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

This is a co~pliment to California Masonry which is appreciated.
A California Mason would be perfectly at home in Arizona Lodges.
It is worthy of note, however, that Arizona Masons are reducing to
cipher and publishing the Ritual or Work which i.s declared to be C~li­
fornia \Vork: Thus we have the anomaly of Anzdna Masons puttmg
into cipher form their Ritualistic Work, which is identical with the
C~lifornia Work, yet in the Proceedings of 1897, page 223, Grand
Lodge of California, we find the following resolution was adopted:
"Resolved: That the mysteries of Freemasonry have, in all ages
since the first organization of this ancient Order, been taught by
tradition and committed only to the faithful breast, and that all suggestion or propositions looking to a change will be regarded as u11;M~sonic and denied consideration in . this Grarid Lodge.'.'
No fee for affiliation is required in j\rizon11 Lodges.
No Report on Correspondence is published.
The next Communication of the Grand Lodge will be holden in
Prescott, commencing November 10, 1908.
Cyrus Grant Jones (Tempe), G. M.
George J . Roskruge (Tucson), G. Sec.

The reviewer discusses one of Past Grand Master Flint's decisions and asks: "We would like to know where the Brother found
any Masonic teaching to the effect that wine must not be served at
Masonic banquets. We believe the whole matter would be better left
to the Lodge ; ii it wants wine at its banquets let it have some."
It is submitted that Masonic teaching can be found against serving
wine at Masonic banquets. "Temperance which renders the body
tame and governable and turns the mind from the allurement of vice,"
and which teaches the Mason to avoid the contracting of any licentious
or vicious habits," is the first of the four Cardinal Virtues. The Entered
Apprentice is charged as a duty to himself to adopt such "a prudent
and well-regulated course of discipline as may best conduce to the

We quote from the Grand Master's address:

Correspondence with Past Grand Master Flint regarding the San
Francisco fire is published, and the Grand Master says: "The relief

go out to them as brothers of one world-wide Masonic family."
The Grand Master ruled that a candidate with one leg five inches
shorter than the other, no metallic appliances being used, and being
able to perform all requirements, was eligible; otherwise, no, the
matter being left to the Master's discretion.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The report on Foreign Correspondence is by Henry Robertson,
chairman. It is full of interesting matter. Four pages are given
to California. Three pages are given to quoting a part of the report
of the Committee on · Jurisprudence of our Grand Lodge upon the
report of Past Grand Master Hunter on the question of jurisdiction
of certain Lodges in the Hawaiian Islands.
Under Iowa, quotation is made from the Custodian's report on
the proper method of the examination of visitors. It is stated that
they found legislation on this subject very limited. We quote a
part of that quotation:
"There is, however, throughout all the Jurisdiction a similarity
found and sameness, in some respects, as that of using a test oath,
or Tyler's oath, varying in form and somewhat in substance, but
quite alike in the essential parts. All work through Committees
appointed for that purpose. * * * We do not find that any Grand
Jurisdiction has found it expedient to make definite rules or prescribe
definite forms for the government of such committees (of examination)
in the performance of their duties. The manifest thought being that
the conditions' cannot "be so far prejudged as to render such rules
or forms of practical utility," etc.
Brother Robertson joins in the discussion in different parts of
his report as to who was the first Grand Master, and also as to when
Speculative Masons were first admitted to Lodges of Operative Masons.
He quotes on the subject of Grand Master an interesting contribution
from Brother W. Holt Apgar, New Jersey, 1905. On the subject
of Speculative Masonry he quotes Brother Cunningham, Ohio, 1905.
There recently died in this State a Masonic scholar, Brother
Salton Frederick Calhoun, who at the time of his death was a member
of one of the Lodges of this Jurisdiction. He was a member of the
Correspondence Circle, Quatuor Coronati Lodge, No. 2076, England.
He ,published a book entitled Historic Masonry in 1899. We quote
a few passages from this book :
"It 'is perhaps · impossible to assign an accurate date for the
admission of non-professional . men into the Lodges of FreemaSOJ'\.S,
prior to the close of the sixteenth century. The earliest authentic
record is to be found on the rolls of Saint Mary's Lodge, at Edinburgh, where it is registered that John Boswell, of Auchinleck, was
present at an assembly of the Lodge in 1600, and that Robert Moray,
a quartermaster-general of the Scottish Army, was admitted as Master
in the ·year 1641.
" In the year 1670, according to the Harleian manusl'ript, the
words, 'accepted a Freemason,' were used to distinguish a Mason
so received and taken by the Frnternity without professional apprenticeship, from one who was initiated because of his vocations, and
this signification is corroborated by Dr. Plot."
Reference is made in Brother Calhoun's book to the Act of 1356.
in the thirtieth year of Edward III, forbidding certain combinations

of the black ball, and says in part : "After twelve months' experience

the Grand Master of Indiana, 1907, and the Grand Master of Delaware, 1906.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

The Grand Master reports the return by Past Grand Master
Hart of California of $788.28 from the relief fund, and recommends
that it be placed in the general fund of 'the Masonic' Home of
Connecticut.

The Re.port on Correspondence is full and very interesting Si
pafges are given to California, 1906, but want of space forbids f~rthe~
re erence here.

16

Edward E. Fuller (Tolland), G. M.
John H. Barlow (Hartford), G. Sec.

The Grand Master calls attention to certain matters · which · he
says should receive consideration. We quote:
"We feel that the practice of encouraging young Masons to
advance as rapidly as possible through the several degrees of Lodge,
Chapter, Council and Commandery, in order that they may join the
Order of Mystic Shrine, is wrong." Again: "Officers should become
proficient, not only in the Ritual, but they should as well, and carefully, prepare themselves for questions of Law and Lodge Government."
The rules and regulations of the Grand Lodge were revised
and adopted and are set forth in full in the Proceedings. We
quote parts of them which will be interesting to California Masons:
Sec. 12. The introduction of spirituous or malt liquors upon
the premises of any Lodge within this Grand Jurisdiction is hereby
strictly prohibited.
Se~. 14. . The minimum fees for degrees are E. A., $10; F. C., $5;
Master Mason, $5. (In the California Jurisdiction the minimum fee
for the three degrees is $30.)
Sec. 21. Every Mason and every Lodge is bound to afford
temporary relief to a sick or distressed Brother, and has no legal
claim for remuneration.
Sec. 22. A Lodge cannot be opened on the E. A. degree in the
first instance. The proper course to follow is to open a M. M. Lodge,
call it off, arid then open upon the degree to be worked. The
work completed, the Lodge must be closed on that degree to be
worked. The work completed, the Lodge must be closed on that
degree and called on again in the M. M. degree for the purpose of
closing in Due Form.
Sec. 30 gives form of petitions for degrees which seems to be
identical with that used in California.
Sec. 35-5. A petitioner for the degrees of Masonry, who is a
Roman Catholic, should be informed that the policy and rules of his
church prohibit his taking such a step ; that the vows of Masonry·
will not permit him to divulge Masonic secrets at confession or elsewhere ; if he then is willing to promise allegiance to the Order, "religious belief" does not constitute a basis for his rejection.
Sec. 30-7. A candidate rejected in any Lodge in this Grand
Jurisdiction cannot renew his application until the expiration of six
months from the date of his rejection.
Sec. 36. Making known the rejection of a candidate to any person
not a Mason, except to the candidate himself, is a Masonic offense.
Sec. 36-2. · When an applicant has been rejected in another Grand
Jurisdiction, he must obtain the consent of the Lodge holding jurisdiction before he can be admitted to a Lodge in this State.

One Hundred and First Communication, Wilmington, Oct. 3, 1906.

quote a few of them:

Levin I. Handy, G. M.
No. of Lodges, 22.

No. of Members, 2,772.

The Grand Lodge of Delaware was organized in 1806. A special
Communication was held at 'vVilmington, June 7, 1906, there being
several eminent Grand Officers of other Jurisdictions in attendance
to celebrate the Centennial Anniversary. A volume of the Centennial
Proceedings is sent out, containing, among other things, a very fine
address by Brother J. P . Dolliver, United States Senator from Iowa.
In this address emphasis is laid upon the dignity of labor, and that
to work is a Masonic teaching. We wish that every one could read
that address. 'vYe quote from it a few sentences: "Civilization is a
labor question altogether." "Everybody that lives in this world is
under a high obligation to work out his salvation in some definite,
effective and· practical way." "A man that does not work, either
with head or hand, is properly described as a dead-head in the
enterprises of society."

In this address he refers to a visit made to the cabin in . which
the mother of Abraham Lincoln was living at the time he was
born, and says: "I stood there with my hat in my hand in silence
and in reverence before all that is left of that rude cabin which
sheltered the infancy of the mightiest man that ever lived in the·
tide of time-that cabin more royal than all the palaces of the earth.
It did not shelter the childhood of a king, but there· is in this world
one thing, at least, more royal than a king-it is a man. For hours
I stood there, and I said to myself, 'This is the American type,' for
you can open the history of the United States anJwhere and you
will not find a name in it that does not have behind it that background of discipline and hard work."

The Report ~n Correspondence is by H. L. Jackson, Past Deputy
G. M. It comprises 87 pages of interesting matter.
In discussing California, quotations are made from the address
of Past Grand Master Hunter.'

The respect which Masonry has for the workman and its elevation of the dignity of labor is one oi its chief claims to human regard.
Are there not too many who believe that the object of work is to
be delivered from work instead of that one object of work is also
service to others? Is there enough emphasis laid upon the great
truth that work and service are the essence of our Christian civilization? Are not the great lessons too often overlooked, that "He who
would be greatest among you shall be servant of many." "I came
to minister, not to be ministered unto." (We quote from memory.)
Perhaps no episode in the history of our race is of more significance
than that of the great Teacher taking the basin and towel and washing his disciples' feet.

DISTRICT OF COLUMBIA.
Ninety-seventh Communication, Washington, March 9, 1907.
No. of Lodges, 31.

No. of Members, 8,363.

A Special Communication was held June 8, 1907, and the cornerstone of the New Masonic Temple laid. The work of laying the
corner-stone, as given by the various officers, is printed in full in
the Proceedings. The addresses made are given, including one by
Brother Theodore Roosev.elt, President .of the United States. The
gavel, trowel and square used were the identical ones used by President Washington at the laying of the corner-stone of the Capitol,
September 18, 1793: he was Acting Grand Master of Maryland on
that occasion. These implements were loaned for the occasion by
the three Lodges to which they had been given by Washington,
and in whose continual possession they have since remained. After
which, the implements having been examined and passed through
· the hands of President Roosevelt, they were returned to their respective owners. The new Masonic Temple is to be six stories high,
with the first story 30 feet in the main auditorium. It is in the classic
style of architecture. The building is to be of stone, and the contract
price for its erection is $344,000.

FLORIDA-1907.
Seventy-eighth Communication, Jacksonville, Jan. 15, 1907.
No. of Lodges, 166.

No. of Members, 7,228.

The Grand Master in his address set forth the correspondence
with Past Grand Master Flint about the San Francisco fire, and says:
"On the 3d of October I received the following telegram, which
speaks for the kindness of heart and brotherly feeling of M.'. W:.
Brother M. H. Flint :
"Los fi:ngeles, Cal., October 3, 1906.

"Chas. W. Johnson, Grand Master,
"Jacksonville, Fla.
"Have been endeavoring to ascertain true condition at Pensacola
and other points from newspaper dispatches, same unsatisfactory.
If there is anything on earth that you require, financially or otherwise, wire me promptly, and immediate assistance will be given
by wire.
"MOTLEY H. FLINT,
"Grand Master."
The Grand Master set forth correspondence showing a movement of the United Daughters of the Confederacy to buy and care
for the Confederate graveyard on Johnson's Island, Ohio, where
206 Southern soldiers were buried during the Civil War. Of these,
152 were Masons. The Grand Master states that about 15,000 Confederate prisoners, almost exclusively officers, were confined there
during the Civil War. The prisoners who were Masons formed what
was known as the Masonic mess. Every two weeks a Lodge-meeting
was held. The Grand Master says:

The corner-stone of the uew Temple was laid January 22, 1908,
by the Grand Master and the Brethren. Interesting addresses were
delivered by Brother Fletcher and Dr. . Yerger, the Grand Orator. We
quote a part of the Grand Orator's address:
"Brethren: The impression prevails that Masonry is a religion
or a substitu e for religion ; that impression is due, perhaps, to such
causes as the following :
"First, that Masonry has a Ritual.
"Second, that the building used is called a Temple.
"Third, that some of the Craft express themselves in such terms ,
as 'Masonry is religion enough for me.'
"As to the first, a religion may or may not have a ritual, and
there may be a ritual not necessarily connected with religion. As
to the second: Temple means a certain circumscribed area devoted
to religious purposes. No one supposes that such a meaning attaches
to .the building used by Masons; they use the word simply from
historical association. As to the third, sometimes silly ·sheep stray
foto the Masonic fold and the Craft, as such, is not responsible for
their bleatings.
"No; Masonry is not a religion, nor does it interfere with any
man's religion. It treats with respect the church, the synagogue· and
the mosque. It meddles not with religion nor with politics; it is
a great moral, benevolent organization. But while not a religion nor
a political system, it has a creed and a platform. A cardinal article
of its creed is integrity, and a plank of its platform is uprightness
of life."
Brother Wright, chairman, writes the report of the Committee
on Correspondence. In his introduction he says: "It is no light
task to read the sixty odd volumes of Proceedings presented for
review and make intelligent excerpts of their contents. There are
thousands of pages of interesting and valuable Masonic literature

We quote from his conclusion:
"The question of requiring documentary evidence o( all applicants
for examination for initiation is spreading, and it will be well for all
Masons to carry at all times receipts for dues, with seal of their
Lodge attached, and a diploma or certificate by the Grand Secretary,
that it is from a Regular Lodge. The Grand Master of Nova Scotia
was refused an examining committee in Boston because he had no
documentary evidence with him. Many others have met with the
same fate when away from home and unknown."
Elmer E. Haskell (Palatka), G. M.

Under California, in the Report on Correspondence, we quot e
the following reference to Past Grand Master Hunter's decision, and
the comments thereon :
"Documentary evidence alone, no matter of what character, is not
sufficient to admit a visitor, but he must prove himself by a personal
examination. 'Vhere, however, he has a statement from the Secretary
of a Lodge, under seal, that he is a Master Mason in good standing,
and is unable to stand a rigid test, very slight evidence by examination should be sufficient to admit him.
"We hardly approve the above. A visitor has no right to present
himself at the door of a Lodge unless he can pass the most rigid
test that can be imposed upon him. We have little use for documentary evidence, but we fi rmly believe that no brother has a right
to travel unless he can 'make good' when put to the crucial test of
rigid examination."
The above paragraph expresses the ideas of the reviewer. We
do not agree with him that a visitor should not be admitted "unless
he can pass the most rigid test that can be imposed upon him."
The purpose of examination is not that the visitor may show proficiency as a Mason, but that he may prove that he is in fact a
Mason entitled to visit a Lodge. The true purpose of the examination is to ascertain that fact. The want of proficiency is often an
evidence of sincerity on the part of the applicant. When a visitor
shows proficiency then the greatest care should be taken; impostors
rarely, if ever, attempt to visit Lodges without such preparation to
meet examinations as would give proficiency, while an honest Mason
relying upon the fact that he is entitled to the privilege often neglects
to prepare himself to pass examinations. The question of the admission of visitors should be left largely to the Lodge, acting through
its Master and Examining Committee ; and such right should not
be denied or abridged upon slight grounds, or because of arbitrary
rules or the failure to conform to some specific regulation.

From the Report of the Committee on Correspondence we quote:
"Queensland is a British colony occupying the whole of the northeastern portion of Australia. The whole of Queensland comprises
678,000 square miles, nearly eight times the area of Idaho.
"The territory of Queensland was occupied by three District Grand
Lodges, presided over by three District Deputy Grand Masters, holding
allegiance respectively to England, Scotland and Ireland. There were
158 subordinate Lodges working under the three constitutions above
mentioned-63 English, 69 Scotch, and 26 Irish.
.
"Two efforts were made to establish a Grand Lodge in Queensland-one in 1887 and the other in 1897-without success. March 23,
1904, a convention of delegates was held at Brisbane, at which ·36
Lodges, 22 belonging to the Irish constitution and 14 to the Scottish,
were represented. At a second convention held April 2S, 1904, ~he
final steps were taken, there being present representatives from 2S
of the 26 Irish Lodges and 14 Scottish Lodges.
"Notice of the movement was sept to every Lodge under the
English, Scotch and Irish constitutions in Queensland. It might be
said in passing that the discussion of the proposition was forbidden
in the Scotch Lodges and was so hedged about in the English Lodges
that discussion was scarcely possible. However, 14 Scotch Lodges 1
decided to join in the movement, their Deputy Grand Master to the
contrary notwithstanding. This left 119 Lodges in Queensland which
took no part in the movement."

The Grand Lodge of Alberta was recognized.
The oration of Brother Owen Scott, Grand Orator, is printed.
One cannot read· such an address without being humbled yet lifted
up in aspiration and the desire to live more worthily as a man.
We quote .the following from it:
"The first and greatest aim of Masonry is toward a loftier fodividual manhood, a purer womanhood, and a more tender and promising childhood. That Masons are builders can be seen by the name.
While the operative craitsman uses perishable brick or stone and
cements it into one common mass, the speculative workman uses living
stones, which when properly united with the ceme.nt of brotherly love
·
and affection constitutes an edifice eternal in the heavens.
"By · teaching men the doctrines of temperance, fortitude, prudenea
and. jus.tice, together with the many other lessons drawn from. and
daily applicable to, the activities of life, deep foundations are laid
upon which loftiest charact~r must stand. When brotherly love, relief,
and truth really enter into the fiber of a man's being, there is little
room for the selfish and the debased. His instincts and his aspira·
tions are toward the uplift that comes from a joyful service to mankind. That
'I Am My Brother's Keeper'
is demonstrated in every avenue of life, whether I am ready to concede it or not. He who achieves fortune, fame, or power over the
crushed form of his fellow has made a Mephisto bargain and will
render his grievous service tn the Inferno of his own creation. . Service
and sacrifice are the crucible in which the base metals of greed, avarice,
and selfishness are left as the dross of life. If thy brother would
have thee go with him one mile, that is thy duty. When to this is
added gladly, a second mile, that is a blessed privilege.
"Masonry has not been concerned with the dogmas of theology
and the factional feuds of rival sects. The church, organized religiou1
thought and activity, stands supreme. To this we reverently bow
modestly claiming the privilege of casting out the devils of human need
in the name of the Master of Men.
"The product of Judaism and Christianity, the Holy Scriptur~
i.s the great light of :Masonry. A belief in God and His Book it
fundamental. Hence no atheist can become or remain ·a Mason and
be honest. \Vhen he ceases to rely upon God as the Supreme Archittct
of the Universe, he owes it to himself and to the Craft to go out
from us, because he is not of us."

· · th
of the Grand
This Communication marked the nmetle . yea.r
Lodge. The Grand Master's address opens with this sentence:

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCF.

35

"In the beautiful spring-time, when nature is bursting forth with
bud and blossom, our Grand Lodge meets, and this year the honor
and the privilege is mine of welcoming you to this session of the
Grand Lodge at a time when there are more Lodges and more
members than ever before in the ninety years of its history."
The Grand Master reported the sum of $2,148.75 on hand raised
for California Masons, but not sent because word had been received
that no. more was needed. Five thousand seven hundred and nineteen
dollars and fifty cents had already been sent.
The Grand Master speaks of the abuse of the black ballot, and
says:
"Masters have appealed to m~ to kn ow if there was not some
method of stopping this fearful scourge; Brethren, because of some
grievance, either real or imaginary, decide to block the wheels of
progress in their Lodge, and by being punctual in attendance are
enabled to vote against any and all applicants. Such conduct is base
and wholly unworthy of our profession as Masons. As the ballot
must of necessity be secret and sacred, we must depend on the honor
and good sense of our membership."
The Committee on Jurisprudence, to whom was referred this
part of the Grand Master's address, said:
"Members of our Lodges, in many instances, no doubt have
exercised this privilege without due regard to the obligations that
rest upon them. A little reflection should aid such members abou't
to cast a black ball against an applicant for membership because of
some personal and trivial reason, to avoid the consequent injury to
themselves and to the Lodge to which. they belong. No one has a
right to do wrong knowingly, and when one knowingly does wrong,
his own higher and better nature sits in judgment and reproves and
condemns. The liberty we possess should not be abused. \Ve should
so use what we possess as not to injure the property of our neighbors. We should so exercise the rights and privileges we enjoy as
Masons as not to wantonly work injury to those that are seeking for
light in Masonry. The use of the black ball, like many other benign
privileges we possess, may be abused. We should not bring our
personal grievances into the Lodge. If we do, we cause great harm
to the institution we profess to love and revere."
It was declared to be the established and uniform custom in
Indiana that in case of widows or or.p hans residing without the
Jurisdiction of the Lodge of which the husband and father was a
member, and in case ·of sickness or ·death of a Master Mason sojourn1ng or residing without the Jurisdiction of his Lodge, that· the relief
dispensed should be by the Lodge within whose Jurisdiction the
Mason, widow or orphan, is at the time the relief is needed.

1906.
Thirty-third Communication, Ardmore, August 14, 1906.

R. W . Chope, G. M.
The Grand Master refers to the wonderful strides of Masonry
made during the previous year, stating that seventeen new Lodges
were formed. Steps were taken for the merger of the Grand Lodge
of Indian Territory with the Grand Lodge of Oklahoma.
Steps were taken towards securing a location for the Masonic
Home.
An oration out of the ordinary was delivered by the Grand
Orator Talmage on "A Design on God's Trestle-board." We quote
from it:
"'Tis a thrilling thought that our own America is leading the world
in Masonic activities. Inspiring to us is the additional fact that the
youngest State in the Union is in the fore-rank shouting to the world to
follow on to victory.
·
"I~ seems that i~ the reserved la!1d of A~erica and in the youngest
State m that promised land, the highest aim of God in nature and
humanity finds freest access to men's hearts."
In thi.s oration the Orator makes the following statement in
regard to· our acquisition of the Louisiana Territory:
"Our administration hastened to ascertain if privilege might be
granted us by apoleon t~ l~nd at New Orleans. Only docking privileges, and they of a very limited character was all that we were asking
for. :W~ei:i the matt~r was taken befor.e Napoleon's minister, that stubborn md1v1dual was m the act of refusmg even this small request when
the Emperor appeared and shot this unexpected question at our minister:
'How would you like to buy the whole Louisiana territory?' That was
the first we ever heard of the idea. Wise Providence who directs the
affairs of nations, as a chess player moves his pawns, had checked the
treasury of France and Napoleon needed money then more than he
needed land in the west and for a pittance we purchased the heart of
America at a time when we began to need it."

Past Grand Master Thornburg of Arkansas was present and
made some interesting remarks, saying in part:
"I can never enjoy a meeting of the Grand Lodge of Arkansas like
I can one where I am visiting, for my time is so occupied with business
and I have so many duties that I have not time for enjoyment. I am
a Past Grand Master, Past Grand High Priest, Past M. P . G. M., Past .
Grand Commander of the Commandery and Past Grand Patron of the
Eastern Star, so you see that I have had duties that kept me busy."
In conclusion he says that "It (Freemasonry) bears upon its
rolls the names of thousands of God's noblemen, the greatest and
truest men on earth, and among them are the names of Washington,
LaFayette, Warren, Franklin, Jackson, McKinley, Roosevelt and
William Jennings Bryan."
The report of the Joint Committee on Merging the Grand
Lodges of Indian Territory and Oklahoma is given. Commenting
upon it Grand Master McBride says the propositions are not tenable,
and says in part :
·
"The United States Government will possibly-at least we are
fondly hoping for it-wipe out these dividing lines, forever obliterating
Indian and Oklahoma Territories by creating the State of Oklahoma.
"There can, then, be no question of 'Mother' Indian Territory
receiving 'Daughter' Oklahoma T~rritory back to !he deserted hon:iestead · nor is the 'Mother' breaking up housekeeping to go and hve
with the 'Daughter,' but mutual concessions must be made and a fraternal union established on which we shall proceed to erect the Grand
Lodge of the great new State of Oklahoma, rebuilding this temple without the sound of iron discord or wooden strife.
"Brethren to me, it is simply a plain case of taking down the cross
fence throwin'g both herds into one pasture and rebranding. The I. T.,
and 0. T. brands will have to be laid aside and hereafter the Masonic
.
ranch of the coming great State will use the plain 'Circle O' brand.
"When the powers that be confer upon this people the inestimable
boon of Statehood we shall see this Masonic union consummated with
·
dispatch and harmony.
"Until this much desired legislation is an assured fact, the discussion of attending details is, in my judgment, premature."

IRELAND.
1906.
The 19Ci6 Annual Report contains a striking group picture of
four Irish Masons, W. J. Chetwode Crawley, Sir Jas. Creed Meredith, H. E. Flaveel, and Rev. Benjamin Gibson. The first two are
men of international reputation among Masons. The report consists
only of statistics and the address of Deputy Grand Master Sir James
C. Meredith, delivered at Dublin on St. John's Day, 1906. We make
the following extracts from his address :
"In North Munster a new Lodge room has been built in Nenagh
In. Limerick there exists a Masonic Club, which has a large member~
ship. The Grand Master of the Province of North Munster Sir Charles
B:irri~gton, Bart., has informed me that Lodge No. 13, ii; the city ·of
Limerick possesses two very valuable antiquities-one a large silver
cup.-the other ~hat is stated to be the oldest known Masonic Jewel.
This latter c1ons1s.ts of. a smal! brass .squ:l;re, fou.nd during the taking
down of Balls Bridge, m the city of Limerick, which was a very ancient
~tructure, and was ~aken down in 1823. This jewel is dated 1517, that
1~ as closely as possibly 400 years ago, and it bears upon it this ir.~crip­
tton :
'I will strive to live with love and care,
Upon the level and by the square.'
which, I think, establishes the Masonic connection of that jewel."
"I mentioned earlier in this address that a terrible earthquake had
~ccurred and had cau~ed the destruction of the City of San Francisco
m the early part of this year. I am very thankful to say that owing to
the energy of our Grand Treasurer, we were the first Masonic body ta
communicate with our Brethren in San Francisco, and to tell them that
thi.s poor little island of ours was sending them by wire one hundred
gum.eas to help the Brethren out there, and that more would follow.
Notice went out to the Brethren, and I must say it was very cordially
responded to. The 'more' that followed brought our contribution to
that fund up to 450 pounds or thereabouts. I think that was a very
satisfactory result."
(The underscoring is ours.)
On black-balling he says:
"You are entitled to keep a man out' of your own Lodge for any
reason whatever, but no man, or any body of men, are entitled to say
that any individual man is not to be admitted to Masonry at all, simply
because they do not like the way in which he follows his profession, or
his trade, or his calling. So long as a man honestly earns his livelihood,
whether he treads upon the corns of others or not, they have each of
them individually the right to keep him out of the Lodge of which they
are members, but collectively they have no right to say that that man
is not to be admitted a member of the Masonic Order. I am assuming
that what he is doing is perfectly lawful, and that he is not doing a nything that is improper, in anything more than professional impropriety.''

KENTUCKY-1907.
One Hundred and Seventh Communication, Louisville, Oct. 15, 1907.
Samuel K. Veach, G. M.
Past Grand Master Thomas Todd was presented and resolutions
in his honor were adopted. He was 87 years old. "He was made a
Mason over sixty-five years ago and has been continuously a member
of Solomon Lodge, No. 5, ever since. More than fifty-four years
ago he was elected Grand Master of Kentucky Grand Lodge, which
he first attended as Representative sixty-one years ago, and has been
present at every one of its sessions since that good year. The Grand
Secretary presented him with a vase of flowers as symbols of fragrant
memories and emblems of our hope."
Grand Master Veach said :
"There never was an era when our great fraternity was so prosperous the world over as now, and our own Grand Lodge is participating in this great prosperity. But we should not forget that with all this
prosperity comes a corresponding weight of responsibility, and as we
come now, at the end of another year, to review our labors of the past
and lay our plans for the future, let us do all with an eye single to
the glory of God and in the uplifting of humanity; and let us remember

44

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

that very soon we must each one for himself, answer the call of the
Grand Warden· of heaven."
"Several Grand Masters have recommended that documentary evidence of membership be required before examination of visitors, and as
many times this Grand Lodge has ignored the recommendation. Notwithstanding this, f again recommend that this Grand Body require
documentary evidence of visitors, and that the matter be referred to
the Committee on Jurisprudence with instructions to prepare and present
a suitable regulation on this subject."
We quote from the Grand Secretary's report as follows:
PRINTED PROCEEDINGS.

"A pamphlet soon becomes unsightly, and its leaves are lost, even
when care is taken; I therefore recommend that Lodges be furnished
with bound copies of the Proceedings, which will not cost over $150
extra, including the postage; then require the Lodges to have a suitable
case for their preservation and convenient use. It seems to me, inasmuch as the Lodges pay for the printing, they are entitled, to books that
will be sightly and in condition to stand the wear of ordinary use.
" If the printed Proceedings that cost $1,300 or more annually are
worth the money expended, they are worth preserving, and ought to be
in possession of Subordinate Lodges for whose benefit the printing is
done. A few Lodges keep them in cases; others have no receptacle for
them. Those that can not afford to procure regular bookcases, can
make a box, or cut a large box down to proper size, affix hinges and a
lock to the lid, turn the box on its side so the lid will be in front, and
put it on brackets at convenient height in the N. E. corner; paint it,
or cover it with nice wall paper, and it will be a very sightly and useful
case. It should be about three feet long, 11 inches high, by 8 or 9
inches deep from front to back, inside. When . full, another like it can
be put on top."

The Grand Master reported twenty-nine decisions; the twentyfifth raises the·_question as to when a Mason dimitted for over a
year, against whom charges had been made, should be tried. The
Grand Master, with the concurrence of the Committee on Jurisprudence, whose opinion he ·gives in his address, decided that he could
be tried only by the Grand Lodge. We quote from their opinion
given in the Grand Master's Report as follows:
"As a rule the 'sojourning' Brother is a member of some Lodge
in some other Jurisdiction; an unaffiliated Brother belongs to no
Lodge and owes no duty to any Lodge. He is under the jurisdiction
of the body at large-the Grand Lodge.
"Now as the unaffiliated Mason owes no duty to any particular
Lodge, what punishment can the . Lodge inflict? It cannot suspend
and it cannot expel, because he 1s not a member. It cannot expel
him from the privilege of Freemasonry; that only the Grand Lodge
can do. From all of which it would seem that only the Grand Lodge
can try and punish, as it may deem proper, a dimitted Mason * * *
"In confirmation of the view that the Grand Lodge may be the
one authority to deal with a non-affiliated Mason, we .refer i!' ~on­
clusion to Mackey, page 275, paragraph 8, on the status of d1m1tted
Masons as follows :
"'And lastly, as. non-affiliation is a v.i<:lation of. M_a sonic .la~, he
may, if he refuses to abandon that cond1t1on, be tned and pumshed

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE:

He submitted the following question to the Grand Lodge: "Can
a Mason, whether an E. A., an F. C., or a M. M., be tried by a
Lodge for an offense alleged to have been committed before he was
made a Mason?" On this subject the Grand Master says:
"In the applications of today the candidate says that he knows
of no physical, legal or ;noral reason why he should not be made
a Mason.
"My own opinion is that the question should still be answered
'No.' What does a candidate know about the physical, legal or moral
reasons which debar him from becoming a Mason? Ask yourselves
the quesiion, what is the fixed moral standard by which a candidate
must measure himself and by which we measure him?
" Practically each candidate must come up to the moral standard,
which each Brother who votes upon him applies to him. If a candidate in his application misstates his residence or his age, or denies
a previous rejection, it is in either case a clean-cut falsehood, and
he knows it. For such an offense he can be and ought to be subject
to charges and trial."
We quote again from the Grand Ma.s ter's address:
"This Grand Lodge is opposed to the doctrine, which has lately
appeared, that when a man becomes a Mason he thereby becomes
entitled to be relieved to the full extent of his wants, wheri in distress,
even to his full support. In fact, the Grand Lodge of Maine has
repudiated that doctrine.
.
"This Grand Lodge holds that a Mason's right to relief is limited
by the extent of his distress and by the ability of the Brother who
assists, of which said ability the assisting Brother is the sole judge
under his Masonic obligation."
California for 1905 is reviewed.

body of Masonic law, as it is understood in this Jurisdiction."

be tried by a Lodge for an offense committed before he was initiated.
The Committee .o n Jurisprudence, to whom this question was referred
in 1906, reported that the conclusion of the Grand Master was correct
and in accordance with Masonic law.

t10n

contemporaneous record commences in 1750. There were certain
previous pages left blank for the insertion of documents and items
of history which might be presented to the Grand Secretary during
his administration, and which he might think it desirable to perpetuate
by entering them in the records. They were probably modeled ·after
the records of the Grand Lodge of England. I never saw the latter,
but Grand Master Heard, Grand Master in 1857, 1858 and 1859,
published in Moore's Magazine an article, reprinted afterwards in
connection with the Proceedings of the Grand Lodge for 1871, in
which he gave a fair account, I think, of what he found in the earliest
records of that Grand Lodge. Their early pages were taken up
largely with lists of Lodges, even given the lists of members of those
Lodges. But our records contain nothing of that kind.
"The record proper, as I have said, commences in April, 1750,
nnd in the ten or twelve previous' pages are the deputations to Henry
Price and two of his successors. There is also some account of
the organization, under Price's authority, of the First Lodge in Boston,
which he constituted on the thirtieth of August, 1733.
"We have also the record of the ,'Ancient' Grand Lodge, the
whole of which is contained in this volume which has been recently
hound. We found that it was falling to pieces, and for its preservation we had a new cover put upon it. This Provincial Grand Lodge
was organized by Joseph Warren on the 27th of December, 1769,
under the authority of the Grand Lodge of Scotland. The Grand
Lodge of Scotland was from its inception an 'Ancient' organization.
You know that the ancient organization sprang from certain Irish
Masons, who, about 1738 or 1740, brought to London the Royal Arch
Degree, and they were always very strenuous to have it connected
with the third degree. The proposal and the ritual that they presented and that they claimed to work, did not meet with favor by the
old Grand Lodge. The consequence was that, after c.o nsiderable
wrangling and ill-feeling, a new and opposition Grand Lodge was
started against the old Grand Lodge. The Grand Secretary, Laurence
Dermott, who was a shrewd, able man, took advantage of changes
that are said to have been made in the words of the three degreesof the second to the first degree, in order to detect applicants to visit
their Lodges who belonged to the new association.
"The 'Ancient' Grand Lodge of London was probably organized
about 1751 or 1752. The Grand Lodge of Scotland had always been
friendly to this new movement, and eventually became known themselves as 'Ancient' Masons.
"All these facts seem to me to prove conclusively that our claim
to have had the first regularly constituted Lodge in this country is
sound. That is all we .have ever claimed-that the first regularly
constituted Lodge in America received its authority from Henry Price.
That Lodge was called the First Lodge in Boston. Often in the
records it is described as 'The Mother Lodge.' In 1749 Thomas Oxnard granted a warrant for the second Lodge. In 1783 John Rowe,
Provincial Grand Master, granted a charter for these two Lodges
to unite, upon their petition, and the charter recites in full the request
of these two Lodges, naming the Brethren who were prominnt in
them and ·who signed the petition. That L'Odge is still in existence,
under the name of St. John's Lodge of Boston; certainly the oldest
regularly constituted Lodge existing in this country. It is in a
very flourishing state, one of. the largest Lodges in our Jurisdiction."

and compass with the letter "G" between. This was the Jewe! worn
by H. A. on the day when the Craft lost his services, and which was
subsequently found upon him.

The death of Bro. Thomas Montgomery, R.'.W.".Grand Secretary
of the Grand Lodge for seventeen years continuously, was appropriately noticed by a memorial resolution.
It was decided that under the Masonic Code, Sec. 342,
"A man having one artificial eye but otherwise qualified was not
eligible to receive the Masonic degrees."
We are taught that "Masonry is a progressive moral science";
and that the Masonic virtue of Justice enables us to render unto every
man his just due. The denial of Masonic membership because of physical defects is in many instances a moral wrong, for Masonry is an
Institution so universal in extent, so closely interwoven with the fabric
of society and so much a part of social life, that those who are in
cannot deny to others the right to come in also, except for just reasons. The purpose of Masonry is not to make "signs," but to make
men. The making of "signs" is a means to ari end. Moral defects are
too often overlooked while physical defects are closely noticed. The
writer believes that great injustice has been often done to noble men
by denying them Masonic membership because of some external physical defect. Why should an artificial eye debar a man from Masonry?
In California it is Masonic law that, although a man may lose an eye
by accident, if the sight of the other eye is unimpaired, he is eligible
to become a Mason.
A. 0. Eberhardt delivered a fine oration.
California for 1906 is fully reviewed.

1907.
Eighty-Seventh Communication, St. Louis, Sept. 24, 1907.
David M. Wilson, G. M.
The Grand Master reports sixty-six decisions. One decision was
that a dimitted Mason could not return his dimit to the Lodge from
which he received it and obtain a new one.
The Grand Master objected to laying corner-stones which had no
marks, words or inscriptions whatever to show that they had been
laid by Masons. ·To such corner-stone laying he enters an emphatic
and solemn protest. He states that the Book of Constitutions provides that on laying corner-stones there should appear the name of
the Grand Master and such other particulars as may be deemed necessa ry, among which should always be the inscription that the stone was
laid by the Grand Lodge. He says:
"I stand for the dignity and high importance of Masonry, and
firmly believe that any organization is honored by having the cornerstone of its building laid by the Order, and the least it can do in return
is to let the stone speak for itself."
The Missourian evidently says, even to corner-stones, "Show me."
Grand Orator Bro. W . C. Atwood delivered an oration on "Freemasonry's Mission to the World." It was fine. We quote a few sentences:
"I believe that it is generally understood among men that the ties
of Masonry are strong. We are glad the world thinks so. We want it
to be known everywhere that Freemasonry binds men together in a
Brotherhood that is the more sacred and enduring because of its high
ideals, and its noble conceptions of life. Such a Brotherhood will always be honored. Such a Fraternity will continue to bear its impressive
testimonial to the world as in the past. It will inspire us in many little
ways to 'spread the cement of brotherly love and affection,' which shall
continue to 'unite us into one sacred band or society of friends and
brothers,' among whom no unholy contention should ever exist. Such
a Brotherhood is endowed with the breath of immortality. These loving links that bfnd us are not to be broken by death:·
A set of jewels was presented by Grand Master G. W. Kendrick,
Jr., of Pennsylvania. It seems that some years ago a stranger came
into the Masonic Temple in Philadelphia bringing a set of jewels which
he offered for sale, and on being closely questioned as to how he had
obtained them and about his right to dispose of them, replied that he
had not time to explain just then but would return later and do so.

replevin them." This led to their being sent to Missouri.

1907.
Fiftieth Communication, Omaha, June 4, 1907.

Z. M. Baird, G. M.
He reports the largest increase in the membership in any previous
year, and the largest cash balance on hand also. We quote from his
address:
"To the subordinate Lodges let me suggest: Don't be in too much
of a hurry to pass the honors around. Just because some brother has
been started at the door or in the south is no reason why, regardless
of qualifications, he should be advanced to the Master's chair. I could
cite you several cases in this State where there was once a good Lodge
and a good Master, where now we have a weak Lodge, all because the
present Master, or the one who preceded him, has not endeavored to do
the work, post himself on the law, or is lacking in ability to preside.
Keep your present Master, if he is a good one, until you are sure that
the man who is eligible is better or just as good."
The cost for each resident in the Masonic Home was $189.97.
The following resolutions were adopted by the Grand Lodge:
"Dealings on a board of trade, providing the transactions are bona
fide purchases or sales, and where the intention of the parties is to
deliver the actual commodities, are legitimate. But when the parties
have no intention of delivering the commodities, but speculate upon the
future price, and intend to settle the difference by the market quotations, it constitutes gambling, and is a Masonic offense."
"Transactions commonly known as 'bucket shop deals' are unqualifiedly condemned as gambling, and subject one guilty thereof to Masonic discipline."
The following report of a special committee was adopted:
"We, your committee to whom was referred that part of the Grand
Master's address concerning clandestine Masons, do hereby recommend
that after August 1st, 1907; no Lodge in this Jurisdiction shall receive a
visitor from any Lodge outside of this Jurisdiction unless a Master
Mason, known as such in the Lodge, shall vouch for the visitor as a Master Mason in good standing, or until the visitor, after strict examination,
shall prove himself to be a Mason in good standing; and no such visitor
shall be examined until he produces to the W orshipful Master
of the Lodge, or to the committee .of examination appointed by him, a
certificate under the seal of his Lodge bearing date not to exceed
twelve months prior to the examination, showing that he is a member of
said Lodge in good standing, which certificate shall also be fo~ifi~d. by
a certificate under the seal of the Grand Lodge of the Junsd1ct1on
whence the visitor comes, that the Lodge giving the certificate is a regular Lodge working under the jurisdiction of a regular Grand Lodge,
recognized by the Grand Lodge, A. F. & A. M. of Nebraska.
"And we further recommend that the Grand Secretary be authorized not to authenticate any diploma other than of the form heretofore
adopted by this Grand Lodge, and in the possession of all subordinate

by the blood, the Lord and Giver of life was believed to enter ·into
covenant of friendship with his servant and to deign to enter and dwell
beneath his roof. It consecrated eastern hospitality and made of it a
sacrament, so that the man, though an enemy, once received across the
threshold of the house, was under the protection of its divine guest.
The persecuted man, and even the fugitive fleeing from justice,. if he
could reach and fling his arms across the threshold, found it a sanctuary. Connected with the threshold, a thousand queer customs, crude
and puerile and superstitious to our nature, logical reason, but full of
richest meaning to the simple picture-loving minds of primitive man,
are to be found in the mythology, folk-lore and early history of well
nigh every nation on the face of the earth. So we find ourselves thus
strangely linked to the men that formed the infancy of the race by this
act we have just performed.
"What meaning had it for us? This, surely: We have acted our
assent to the Psalmist's words, 'Except the Lord build the house, their
labor is but lost that build it,' and so we have practiced a precept of the
Order, that no great or important undertaking ought to be entered
upon without first invoking the blessing of Deity. We have prayed
that the work thus begun may be continued and ended in Him."
The Grand Master said in his address to the Grand Lodge at the
Annual Communication in part:
"Now I begin to understand the unity of organization, the unity
of purpose, which holds together our vast Brotherhood, for the happiness and elevation of mankind. Our own Grand Lodge has its sphere of
influence, but its strength and power lies not alone in the number of
its Lodges, in the roll of its membership, but in the mighty hosts that
surround us and whose battle cry is the same as ours, 'Justice to all
and oppression to none.' "
The following decision is reported :
"A diploma of itself is not evidence sufficient to admit a visitor
unless properly vouched for. All applicants for admission to a Masonic
Lodge must, unless properly vouched for, take the test oath and pass
a satisfactory examination by a duly appointed committee for that
purpose."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

"That in the organization of a Grand Lodge, the well s~ttled
American doctrines should govern, viz :
"'That in any unoccupied territory, where a sufficient number of
Lodges (not less than three) exist,. to form a Grand Lodge, such
Lodges shall have the right to organize a Grand Lodge for themselves,
and when thus organized (all proceedings being regular) it is entitled
to recognition.'
·
"We are in receipt of a circular giving notice of an agreement
entered into between the Grand Lodges of England, Scotland and Ireland, as to the question of recognizing a new Grand Lodge.
"The agreement is as follows :
" 'The question of recognizing a new Grand Lodge in :111y colony
or territory in which the three Grand. Lodges have equal jurisdiction,
and have warranted Lodges working therein, shall not be taken into
consideration unless at least two-thirds of the Lodges in each Jurisdiction have signified their adhesion to such new body, and such recognition shall only be granted by agreement of the three Grand Lodges.'
"While we do not question the right of the three Grand Lodges
to determine for themselves the conditions upon which they will recognize a newly-formed Grand Lodge, we do not deem their agreement as
a governing factor as determining for ourselves under what conditions
we will grant recognition.''
Queensland was recognized.

The Grand Master reports laying the corner-stone of a Scottish
Rite Temple in Jersey City, Oct. 27, 1906, when Brother Thomas B.
Dill, 33rd Degree of Hope Lodge, No. 124, F . & A. M., delivered an
address. We quote from it :
"The Blue Lodge is the source of the great Masonic river · that
flows on to the broad ocean that encompasses the earth.
"To every well-informed Mason the symbolism of the cornerstone,
when laid with Masonic rites, is full of significance. That significance
appertains to the form, to its situation, to its permanence, and lastly
to the consecration which we are assembled here today to witness.
"Masonic education and training so leads one to follow that which
is handed down, that in briefly referring to the symbolism of the cornerstone, one may be pardoned for following Masonic authorities even
to the extent of adopting language, making no claim to originality
therein.
"The corner-stone, square on its surface, is symbolical of morality.
In its solid contents a cube, it is indicative of truth. Placed as the
corner-stone is, between the north, the place of darkness, and the east,
the place of light, its position symbolizes the Masonic progress from
darkness to light and from ignorance to knowledge.
"The permanence and durability of the corner-stone, outlasting
the building, reminds the. Mason of the immortality of the soul.
"We have seen here today the stone deposited in its appropriate
place, examined with the necessary implements of operative Masonry-

NEW MEXIC0-1906.
Twenty-Ninth Communication, Albuquerque, Oct. 15, 1906.
James G. Fitch, G. M.
We quote from his decisions:
"1-Held that a member of a Mexican Lodge working the York
. Rite i~ English under charter from Grand Lodge Valle _de Mexi~o, !Ind
who can prove himself to be a Master Mason upon strict examination,
has the right of visitation in this Jurisdiction. The right o! visitation is
a personal one belonging to every Master Mason, p;ov!de.d _he does
not hail from a clandestine Lodge or one under the Junsd1chon of a
Grand Body against which a decree of non-intercourse has been promulgated on account of the violation by such. Grand Body ?f som~ of
the Ancient Land-marks; such decree of non-1.ntercourse bemg eqm".'.!1lent to a declaration that such Grand Body 1s no longer, at least m
some respects, a Masonic Body."
"2 .:_1 made a similar ruling in the case of a visitor from a Mexican
Lodge. under jurisdiction of the Grand Orient of ~exico."
"12.-A minister immediately after being ra1.sed to the dei;rree of
Master Mason was requested to act as Chaplain of the Lodge; he
refused to act unless permitted to close Lodge prayer, 'only in the name
and for the sake of Jesus Christ.'
"Held this was not permissible. Blue Lodge Masonry requires a
belief in God, but no further religious belief; so that all believers in
Deity, whether Christians,. Jews, Mohammedans, are equally eligible
for membership."
Both of these decisions were approved.
Valle de Mexico was recognized for reasons given on p. 49 of the
Proceedings.
The Report on Correspondence is 209 pages and is by P. G. M.
Roth. California for 1905 is reviewed in seven pages. The reviewer
says:
"We desire to thank Brother Davies for his definition of clandestine and irregular Masons."
The amendments to the constitution, by-laws and resolutions
adopted at that Communication are printed in a collective form in a~
appendix. The writer thinks this would be a good practice in the publication of our Proceedings. We have found important resolutions scat•ered through the Pr·oceedings which have the force of regulations, yet
Jo not appear among our printed regulations. Moreover, it is often
difficult, without study, to ascertain from the Grand Master's address
and Report of Committee on Jurisprudence, what has been decided.
. Masters of the Lodges who receive the Proceedings should not be compelled to go through the volume to find in the reports or the recommendations of the officers, the resolutions which are to guide their action. They should be collected and printed together.
No. of Lodges, 26.
No. of Masons, 1,629.
Alpheus A. Keen (Albuquerque), G. Sec.
