1907.
Thirtieth Communication, Carlsbad, Oct. 21, 1907.
A. N. Pratt, G. M.
He reports a decision that a Lodge in New Mexico cannot confer
degrees for a Lodge in Wisconsin under dispensation. Also upon rejection of a candidate for affiliation his <limit should not be so marked.
He decided that there was no law forbidding a petition for a degree
from a person engaged in the liquor business, but quoted a decision of
1902 as follows :
"We consider it highly important that the Lodges should be very
careful in the choice of material, and it is our opinion that generally
speaking persons connected in any way with the liquor business are
undesirable material for our Subordinate Lodges."
This is in line with California decision. In 1900 (see Proceedings
1900, p. 862) the Committee on Jurisprudence in a report which was
adopted, declared that a law forbidding reception of a petition from one
engaged in the sale of intoxicating liquors would introduce class legislation, "a thing repugnant to the fundamental principles of Freemasonry," and continuing, said :
"By one of the unchangeable tenets of our Order each Lodge is
constituted the sole judge of the moral and social fitness of any applicant who knocks at its outer door for admittance. Temperance is one
of the cardinal principles of Freemasonry. Its precepts are inherent
in our ceremonies. They are unchangeable, and therefore, more per·
manent and just as obligatory as the mandates of our Constitution.
The Lodge, or the individual Mason who disregards the requirements
of temperance to such an extent as to injure the good name of Masonry, becomes, by the very force of our traditions, subject to Masonic
discipline. We therefore recommend that the proposed amendment be
not adopted.
Recognition of Queensland was postponed for reasons given in the
clear and able report of Bro. Wroth, Chairman of the Committee on
Correspondence.
The Report on Correspondence reviews California for 1906.
No. of Masons, 1,847.
James W. Wilson (Roswell), G. M.
James H. Wroth (Albuquerque), G. Sec.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

Recognition of the Grand Lodge of Queensland by New South
Wales Grand Lodge offended the Grand Lodge of Scotland, which withdrew its Grand Representative. The minute on the subject sent to-Scotland is calm, dignified and courteous and does _credit to our Brethren
of New South Wales. To those interested in the Queensland discussion
these minutes wili be entertaining.
On April 24, 1906, Admiral Sir Harry Holdsworth Rawson, K. C.
B., was duly installed as Grand Master.
California for 1905 is reviewed.
Arthur H. Bray (Sydney), G. Sec.

Referring to the Home at Utica, the Grand Master says:
"I believe that there should be established at the Home suitable
small industries for the occupation of those whose services can be put
to practical account. Light rug weaving, or kindred work, would afford
opportunities for the exercise of individual taste and in my judgment be
beneficial in maintaining the morale of the establishment."
Speaking of the children in the Home, he says:
. "For our little ones, we did everything and they acquired no practical- ~nowledge of do.mesti.c life. This defect in our system is being
remedied. A Domestic Science plant has been provided, the children
are taught all household duties, the girls make their clothes and hats,
carpenter outfits for our boys are teaching them to use their hands,
·
and other innovations are planned." * * *
"True, this Home question, fhis children question, is a new one for
us, but because it is a very great problem, and because we are charged
with the future ~f ~h~se sixty-five or seventy children today, perhaps
more tomorrow, 1t 1s incumbent upon us to make men and women of
them. They are the children of our Fraternity, their lives must be the
exponents of what our Fraternity stands for. We cannot claim credit
in large measure for the discharge of the duty owing these little ones."
He has inaugurated a system of keeping a record of what becomes
of the children graduated from the Home, and their movements thereafter are kept note of. He says:
"Today no boy or girl leaves that Home but that his or her movements are kept note of. Each is committed to the care of the Lodge
through which admission was obtained to the Home, that Lodge is held
responsible, the children are followed, and we are going to know just
where each child is.
"There are periods in the lives of all young people when they ask
themselves the question, 'Is this battle of life worth while?' When that
question is put hereafter by any of ours, the Home, its influence atmosphere, and welcoming home doors, will all tend to prompt ~ joyful
answer, 'Yes'."
He recommends revision of the Constitution and Code.
Grand Master Scudder was advanced to the floor from Deputy
Grand :\'4aster. His address indicates a man of unusual executive ability. He was re-elected Grand Master, which shows that the New York
Brethren appreciate his services to the Craft.
In the report of the Committee on Masonic Home and Asylum Fund
the hope is expressed that the children in the Home may have an Asylum entirely away from the present Home at Utica, where they are in
contact with the aged and infirm. 'l'he Committee believe that lasting
benefit would result to the children by such action.
The interdict against the Grand Lodge of Hamburg was withdrawn.
Printing for the Grand Lodge costs about $6,000 per year. The
Committee on Printing recommended that bids on printing for the
Grand Lodge be obtained from at least three reputable firms. The following was substituted:
"Resolved, That the matter of printing of the Grand Lodge be left
to the Grand Secretary under the direction of the Grand Master."

NORTH CAROLINA-1907.
One Hundred and Twentieth Communication, Raleigh, Jan. 8, 1907.
F. D. Winston, G. M.
He says not a dispute mars that harmony and peace that makes our
He says "Not a dispute mars that harmony and peace that makes
our Institution strong." He made few decisions. "In most cases a
friendly letter to all concerned has restored harmony." ·
A Masonic Temple is to be built, and $51,000 has been paid in out
of the $89,000 subscribed.
The Grand Master recommended that the District Deputies be
charged with the work of extending the organization of the Eastern
Star, which recommendation was adopted.
The following was among his decisions :
"The fact that a man is a member of the Roman Catholic Church
does not render him ineligible for the degrees of Masonry. We believe
it would be greatly to the benefit of the Order, and certainly give that
great body of zealous Christians a better idea of Masonry if more of
its votaries joined our Order."
There are 280 children in the Orphan Asylum.
The oration was twenty-four pages long, by Grand Orator Cardon.
A corner-stone was laid on April 19, 1906, in Wilmington for a monument by the Society of Colonial Dames in memory of the Cape Fear
heroes of the Revolution.
California for 1905 is reviewed in the Report on Correspondence.

Louis A. Jacobsen, G. M.
He reported the year one of steady growth and prosperity. Four
new Lodges were organized. He decided that a Mason could not hold

upon hearing of the California earthquake he caused the Grand Secretary to write to P. G. M. Dr. Albert Herrick, of Santa Rosa, California,
and immediate steps were taken to aid in the relief work.
The Secretary says in his report that owing to the growth of· clandestine Lodges in this country many Grand L odges are prohibiting visitation from Masons from foreign jurisdictions without a receipt for
dues from their Lodges and an annual certificate from the Grand
Lodges.

1907.
Forty-Second Communication, Halifax, June 12, 1907.
Charles R. Smith, G. M.
At ten o'clock, headed by a band, the Grand Lodge forming a procession, marched to Saint Paul's Church, where a sermon on "Love the
Brotherhood"-! Peter, ii,17 was preached by ' Grc>nd Chaplain G. C.
Wallis. Returning to Freemasons' Hall the Grand Master delivered his
address. He reported $20,000 raised towards establishing a Masonic
Home. About $18,000 of the fund was raised through a Masonic fair.
He reports that at the last Annual Communication the Rite, as practiced in New York, was adopted as the authorized work of the Nova
Scotia Grand Lodge, and continues:
"In pursuance of this resolution I have endeavored to obtain a certified copy of the New York work, but was unable to do so. We were
informed that they had no written or printed work of which they could
give a certified copy, but if this Grand Lodge sent a delegation to New
York they would be most happy to convey the work 'from mouth to
ear.' Not feeling justified in incurring this expense nothing' further
was done in the matter, and it is once more before the Grand Lodge to
deal with it."
Again we quote from his ·address:
"It is not by any means a mistake, once in a while, to have an
'At Home,' or some other social function in our lodge rooms to which
the ladies can be invited. We are not thereby 'playing to the galleries,'
neither are we seeking publicity, for the experience of the past year
shows that the ladies, in the goodness of their hearts. are deeply interested in our work. Encourage, then, my Brethren, this interest, for
anything which appeals to the heart of noble womanhood is for good,
and will be of lasting advantage."

OHI0-1906.
Ninety-Seventh Communication, Columbus, Oct. 10, 1906.
Lewis P. Schaus, G. M.
He says: "Our official circle remains unbroken, no past or present
officer of this Grand Lodge having passed away since last we met." He
mentions the death of Bro. Brenton D: Babcock, of Cleveland, who died
in that city January 10th, 1906, and says:
"Brother Babcock was one of the best known Masons in the United
States, and was as much respected as any man I ever knew. His death
is a loss to the Fraternity and he will be greatly missed by the members
of the Craft, and the bodies of which he was a member."
He warns Lodges against an impostor, one Gamaliel Wad-El-Ward,
who claimed to be a Past Master of Royal Solomon Mother Lodge of
Jerusalem.
We quote from his address :
"Some time ago a Trowel was started by Justice Lodge, of New
York City, in a journey throughout the various Masonic Grand Jurisdictions, and was called the 'Traveling Trowel.' · Each presentation was
made the special feature ·of large social Masonic functions, and the
object to be secured was a further intensifying of Masonic principles,
and the renewing of Masonic friendships.
"In May this Trowel reached Ohio, being presented to the Masons
of this State at Toledo, by the Masons of Michigan. The meeting was
large and enthusiastic, arid it is hoped may result in much good to the
Craft."
He prints the correspondence, showing that Ohio Grand Lodge
acted very promptly and generously in giving aid in our great earthquake calamity.
The following Code amendment was adopted :
"Sec. 25. A member may, by. consent of the Lodge, <limit and until
he again affiliates he voluntarily renounces all claim to the benefit of
Lodge organization. Such a member may at any time within three years,
not having joined any other Lodge, return such <limit to the Lodge
granting it, pay the annual dues since the date of such <limit, and he
may thereupon, if no charges have been preferred against him, be reinstated as a member of such Lodge, if upon a secret ballot, at least
three-fourths of the members voting, shall consent · to such reinstatement."

1907.
Ninety-Eighth Communication, Canton, Oct. 16, 1907.
Horace A. Irvin, G. M.
He says in his address :
"No one who has not been similarly situated can appreciate the
sense of responsibility that comes to a man, with the realization that
he has been called to and accepted the leadership, for a fixed period,
of seventy thousand of the best citizens of the Commonwealth, all
pledged to the highest ideals of right living."
In his decisions he omits the names of persons and Lodges except
where the same is necessary. We learn from one decision of a new
Order which originated in Michigan known as the "White Shrine of
Jerusalem," which is s~id to bear the same relation to the Eastern· Star
that the Royal Arch Chapters do to symbolic Masomy.
He sustained a Master ordering a re-ballot where before the close
of a Lodge after the ballot had been had electing three candidates, on
demand of a brother, an examination of the ballot-box showed all the
black balls glued to the bottom of the ballot-box, and the re-ballot resulted in the rejection of one of the candidates.
From the Report of the Grand Secretary we quote as follows:
"While a number of the Returns for the last .few years have been
sent in typewritten, I am inclined to doubt the wisdom of using the
typewriter for this purpose. I find that in a number of instances the
typewritten Returns have faded out so that they have become almost
illegible and, in some instances, have had to be retraced before they
entirely fade away. A good, permanent ink, which will last for a
century at least, should be used. We have in the office of the Grand
Secretary Ret~rns which were made out in 1809 that are as legible
today as when they were first written, and we surely ought to be able
to find inks today which would prove as lasting as those of a hundred
years ago."
·
He says they are making duplicate copies of these Returns to avoid
the loss arising from their destruction.
.
The Report on Correspondence is by Bro. Cunningham. California
is reviewed at length. His report is very fraternal in spirit. The opening
contains ·correspondence with eminent Masonic scholars, and a brief
discussion on Masonic symbolism and other subjects; also a very interesting paper from the Freemason by Bro. R. F. Gould on "Affiliation
of Speculative Masonry." From this article we note that the late
Brother George W. Speth contended that "The cathedral builders were
a separate class from the Masons of the city guilds or companies."
The inference seems to be that Speculative Masonry came through the
church builders and had an earlier origin· than has lately been believed.
Bro. Cunningham expresses sincere regret at the retirement of
M. W. Brother Davies from the reportorial work of the Grand Lodge
of California.

George D. Copeland (Marion), G. M.

On May 2nd, 1906, the William L. Elkins Masonic Orphanage for
Girls was dedicated; the estimated value of the gift is $400,000.
Representatives of 361 Lodges attended the December Quarterly
Meeting.
It is stated that Franklin's "Mason Book," i. e., Anderson's "The
Constitutions of the Free-Masons," printed in London, in 1723, and
reprinted by Franklin in Philadelphia in 1734, was the first Masonic
.
book printed in America.
In his address the Grand Master speaks of the Masonic Temple in
Philadelphia as "probably the most magnificent structure in the world
dedicated solely to the purposes of our Fraternity." He says:
"In the belief that uniformity of symbols as well as principles in
all ] urisdictions is vital to the success of our Fraternity, I have restored the display of lights upon the Bible on the altar."
Among his decisions, which seem to be final, are these:
"The use of a typewriter for recording the minutes of a Masonic
Lodge is prohibited."
"Dual membership is not permitted. It is not permissible for a
Brother to be a member of two Lodges, at one and the same time
either in this .] urisdiction, or in this and another."
"Subordinate Lodges a re not permitted to correspond with Lodges
in other Jurisdictions."
"I have decided that no Brother could be elected W or shipful Master in a ·Lodge who is not a citizen of the United States."
California for 1905 is reviewed in the Report on Correspondence.
No. of Lodges, 456.
No. of Masons, 75,273.

QUEBEC-1907.
Thirty-Seventh Communication, Montreal, Feb. 13, 1907.
David A. Manson, G. M.
The death of Past Grand Master Edson Fitch is announced.
Referring to the San Francisco fire, the Grand Master says :
"The appalling disaster which visited San Francisco in April last
evoked universal sympathy, and a 1<eneral desire to render aid to the
sufferers by that dire calamity. The subject of contributing to the
relief fund was under advisement when the declaration of the Chief
Magistrate of that country, to the effect that the American people
neither solicited, desired, nor required outside aid, gave a new and
rather peculiar aspect to the subject.
"That to effusively proffer aid tci a wealthy, spirited and selfreliant people, without necessity, and against their expressed wishes,
in the name of Benevolence, would appear, at least to some people, as
of doubtful propriety. I decided to defer action till our line of duty
was more clearly defined."
From the "In Memoriam" on Brother Edson Fitch by P. G. M.
Chambers we quote the following:
"He was the only American citizen, retaining his allegiance as
such, who has occupied the Grand East of Masonry in a British Possession, and this illustration of the fact that Masonry knows no nationality seemed to afford no small degree of pleasure when mentioned
by the writer at a memorable meeting of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, which was attended by Bro. Theodore Roosevelt and by many
hundreds of prominent Brethren of that Grand Lodge and of those of
the neighboring Jurisdictions."
He represented the Grand Lodge of California.
Bro. Chambers, in the opening of his Report on Correspondence,
says the Grand Lodg~ Reviewer,

1908.
Thirty-Eighth Communication, Montreal, Feb. 12, 1908.
Geo. 0. Stanton, G. M.
We quote from the Grand Master's address :
"The amount of good each one does by precept and example is the
truest test of our individual worth to the Order to which we are proud
to belong, while our organization as a whole can only maintain the
standard already reached and succeed in rising to still higher things by
the united efforts of all towards still greater usefulness."
He refers to the custom of attending church services annually by
the Lodges, and says, "I must heartily commend the custom adopted by
these Lodges of attending divine services in a body every year."
We quote again:
"A member of one of our Subordiate Lodges reports having been
unable to obtain admission into a Lodge he wished to visit across the
border. The reason given him being that he was not in possession of
documentary evidence to show he was a Mason of good standing. This
appears to be a rule in many, if not all, Lodges in the United States,
and I deem it advisable to bring the matter before the Grand Lodge."
The net increase for the year in membership is 291 and the cash
receipts the largest in the history of the Grand Lodge.
Bro. Chambers for the nineteenth time writes the Report on Correspondence. Reviewing California for 1907, he says, "Bro. H art's address was an exceedingly eloquent one," and quotes from it. In his

sun, and keeping company with the hours, circles the earth daily with

One Hundred and Sixth Communication, Providence, May 21, 1906.
Joseph W. Freemen, G. M.
The Proceedings contain interesting addresses by M.".W.". Bro.
William H . Scott, M.'.W.". E. H . Rhoades and Bro. Chester W. Barrows at the laying of a corner-stone. We quote from Bro. Barrows'
address:
"Opportunity is all the true man asks, equality of chance with the
boundless future before him, limited only by his capacity to do and to
be. This privilege will not be denied while the humble and mighty
meet around the Masonic board as equal guests and know and feel that
prosperity is doubled, adversity halved, by sharing with one's fellowmen; a truth so beautifully shown in times of sudden and appalling
horror such as have recently occurred in our own fair country.'

SASKATCHEW AN-1907.
First Communication, Prince Albert, June 18, 1907.
H. H. Campkin, G. M.
He says:
"The progress we have made in the past ten months places matters
in a different light from that we had when we formed on the 9th of
August last. I must confess that I did not like the idea of the formation of the new Grand Lodge, and severing from the Grand Lodge of
Manitoba, but, recognizing the great distance our northern Brethren
were traveling in attending Grand Lodge, the great inconvenience to
Grand Lodge Officers, and the distance they had to travel in making
official visits, the great progress of the Western country, it is evident
that our action on the 9th of August was · all for the best."
He says recognition has been asked from California. He refused
a dispensation to initiate a candidate who had lost a foot.
He says in urging attendance at divine services by the Lodges at
least once a year, as is the custom there:
"I wish to state most emphatically that anything that looks like a
severance of Masonry and Christianity cannot but be mischievous to
the best interests of the Craft. Masonry is not Christianity, but it is
so based upon it and so inextricably intertwined with it ,that the two
cannot be disassociated in the minds of right-thinking Masons."
Northwest Mounted Police Lodge, No. 11, was composed entirely
of men of the Mounted Police.
The Secretary reports the number of members, 1,400; number of
Lodges is 37.
H. H . Campkin (Indian Head), G. M.
J. · M. Shaw (Regina), G. Sec.

SOUTH CAROLINA-1906.
One Hundred and Thirtieth Communication, Charleston, Dec. 11, 19C6.
Frank E . Harrison, G. M.
He said:
"Masonic labors are so congenial and pleasant, and peace and harmony so prevalent throughout this Grand Jurisdiction that I am sure
to each of us this Communication will be a happy reunion of friends
und Brothers."
The following amendment to the Constitution was proposed:
"Provided, That such maiming or dismemberment which does not
nctually prevent a candidate from fulfilling all the req,uirements of his
uhligati6ns, shall not be a disqualifying physical disability."
It was defeated, the vote for being 272, against 246; necessary to
carry 346, it requiring a two-thirds vote to amend the Constitution.
'vVe notice that a Brother introduced a constitutional amendment to
the effect that the Constitution can be amended after laying over one
yea r "if the representatives of one-third of the Lodges entitled to repregcntation be present, and the majority of the votes concur."
It was resolved to establish a Masonic Home, and a committee of
five was appointed for that purpose.
The Report on Correspondence is by J. T. Barron, Grand Secretary. California for 1905 is reviewed and quotations made from P. G.
M. Hunter's address. Under North Dakota he quotes the following
from her Grand Secretary :
"In growing old, we find two facts : one that new friendships do
not knit themselves so closely into the tissues of our hearts; and the
other, that an appreciation of friendship comes with a warmer, yet
sadder, light than it did when the world was all before us. We also
come to find that worldly wealth and honors are not the things which
~w eeten the maturer lives, but rather the friends we have made and the
good we have done."

and reared to meet certain needs ~elt in the entire C:aft, a~d . it ~as
fairly met the want whi~h ~rought 1t fo~th. It has achieved d1stmctl?n
in the realms of Masomc ltterature at tJ~es, but that ~as n?t. been its

The Report on Correspondence is by Bro. S. A. Brown. California
for 1906 is reviewed. We quote the following :
"M.".W.".Brother Motley H . Flint, Grand Master. · His picture
opens the volume. It tells nothing to the casual observer. A good
looking, wholese>me, hearty, clean man. One who would be a pleasant
companion, tell a good story, sing a passable song and radiate to you
the old Masonic sentiment, 'Happy to meet, sorry to part, always happy
to meet again.' But Brother Flint is also a hero. Whoever has read
these reports in former years will remember that we have always given
to our California Brethren the Grand Honors on account of their great
benevolence and generosity. Nowhere on the face of the globe have
people been so free and hospitable in relieving the distress of the wayfaring and the destitute. ·It has been like the Knight Templars of old
who wekomed and cared for the pilgrims at Jerusalem, except that they
did not have to say, 'Silver and gold have I none, but such as I have
I give unto thee!' Superabounding wealth was there, and no Mason,
however poor his brand of Masonry might be deemed to be, was allowed to lack by our Brethren of the Golden State.
"So when the great disaster came and the beautiful cities of the
coast were laid in ruins and consumed by fire, it appeared at once that
the well-earned fame of our Brethren for deeds of charity and pure
beneficence had spread both far and wide. Instantly from all the earth
over came the cordial assurance that money and provisions had started
from all points and were speeding their utmost for the Golden Gate.
The generous heart of the world was stirred to its profoundest depths.
"But who was to see that the great hospitality of the Masonic
world should reach is proper guests? It was this hero, Motley H.
Flint, and his noble band of Brothers of the various relief boards who
day and night, forgetting themselves, their business, their families, untiringly labored to direct that hospitable flood of supplies to the intended
board. Verily it is true as set down by our first Most Worshipful
Grand Master,
" 'The liberal soul shall be made fat; and he that watereth shall be
watered also himself.'"
·
No. of Masons, 6,675.
No. of Lodges, 108.
William E. Milligan (Aberdeen), G. M.
Geo. A. Pettigrew (Sioux Falls); G. Sec.

SWITZERLAND-1906.
These Proceedings are in the German language. A small portion
is in English, from which we give what follows. The preface is entitled
Freemasonry in Switzerland, Historic Notes. The first Lodge was
founded at Geneva in 1736.
From the "Principles of the Union of the Swiss Lodges Alpina" we
give the following :
"The Lodge, considered as a Lodge, forbids, both without and
within its bosom, any interference in political and religious affairs.
* * * * On the other hand, each Mason, in his private capacity, is
expected to take an interest in public affairs as a means of affirming· his
Masonic principles."

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.
It is stated:

"Some years ago a Central Mutual Aid Society was founded by the.
Grand Lodge Alpina, which, with the assistance of the Lodges, relieves
the wants of the families of deceased Brethren, or of those that are
in distress of circumstances.
"On the other hand, Freemasons are not under any obligation to
render one another any mutual aid and assistance· in private .life, ·as is
commonly believed."
A Report of the International Bureau for Masonic Intercourse is
published. Its object is stated to be "to establish friendly and easy relations among the various Groups of Universal Masonry." The Bureau
was opened January 1, 1903. Article 1 of its statutes says:
"The International Bureau for Masonic Intercourse is intrusted
with the task of facilitating the relations among the Masonic Powers
without encroaching in any way on their independence and sovereignty."
Dr. H. Haberlin (Zurich LV.), G. M.
Dr. Ad. Streuli (Zurich I), G. Sec.

TENNESSEE-1907.
Ninety-Third Communication, Nashville, Jan. 30, 1907.
Robert Burrow, G. M.
He reports sixty-seven official rulings. On physical defects he
rules that:
"The question as to whether a candidate is a fit subject physically
for Masonry is one primarily for the Lodge. If capable of receiving
and imparting the ritual of Masonry he is eligible."
The Committee on Jurisprudence reporting on the matters set forth
in the Grand Master's address referred to them, said:
"The consistent and courteous refusal · of the Grand Master to
allow himself to be used either officially or personally as a tribunal for
the expression of opinion on abstract questions of Masonic law merits
commendation and affords an example in the conduct of a great office
which, if resolutely followed, will afford his successors time in their
busy lives to attend to the serious and onerous duties of practical
administration."
The death was announced of P. G. M. Sloan. A beautiful memorial
by Grand Chaplain Brother Stowe contains the following:

lonely camp fire, encircled by the dark arid silent woods, while overhead the . far constellations swung through the infinite fields of space,
seeming to feel the sweet influence of. the Pleiads and to be bound by
the bands af Orion.

UTAH-1907.
Thirty-Sixth Communication, Salt Lake City, Jan. 15, 1907.
S. W . Badcon, G. M.
He reports that on April 19, 1906, he wired P. G. M. Flint, "Masons of Utah are with you in sympathy and will work under your instructions." He refers to the good work done by Weber Lodge, No. 6,
of Ogden, saying :
"As soon as it was reported· that many of those who had been
made homeless and destitute by the awful calamity would be sent east
from San Francisco via the Southern Pacific Railway, and that Ogden
would be the first stopping place, the members of Weber Lodge were
organized into committees under the direction of the Worshipful Master,
Bro. C. D. Ives, and for days and nights met every train and assisted
in furnishing the sufferers with raiment and food."

He reports one decision, which was 'approved, namely: That a
Worshipful Master cannot alone examine a Brother for visitation .. He
must appoint a committee of not less than two Brothers. The California ruling is that the Master has ·discretion to admit or exclude visitors.

VERMONT-1906.
One Hundred and Thirteenth Communication, Burlington, June 13, 1906.
Walter E. Ranger, G. M.
He says:
"Throughout this Jurisdiction there are abundant evidences of the
worthy life of the ·Fraternity and of the wondrous power of Masonry
to ennoble mankind. Everywhere there is a reverent appreciation of
its sublime truths, its inspiring beauty and its vivifying spirit. In the
conduct of life the Brethren shadow forth high Masonic ideals. Light
shines brightly from our many altars. With hardly an exception peace
and prosperity reign everywhere. * * * *
"Vermont has one Mason for every thirty inhabitants, or a Mason
for e>'ery eight men of lawful age. So far as I know, no sister Jurisdiction excels us in Masonic strength, either in the number of Masons relative to population or in the sterling manhood of our Masonic citizenship."
Progress was reported in the establishing of a Masonic Home. The
Grand Master closes with this verse :
" i\h, when shall all men's R'O od
Be each man's rule, and universal peace
Lie like a shaft of light across the land,
And like a lane of beams athwart the sea,
Thro' all the circle of the golden year."

WASHINGTON-1906.
Forty-Ninth Communication, Spokane, June 12, 1906.
Abraham L. Miller, G. M.
He reports:
"That the condition of the Craft throughout this Grand Jurisdiction
is especially gratifying. The year has been uneventful; hardly a ~l?ud
has appeared to cast a shadow over the peace and harmony preva1lmg.
The steady increase of our membership has kept pace with the strenuous
spirit which seems to permeate this Northwestern country. New Lodges
have been formed, and a healthy growth has prevailed in the chartered
Lodges, with very few exceptions. The futu·re of Masonry never seemed
brighter."
He reports twenty decisions. We give the following :
"A Brother cannot become a member by affiliation in another Lodge,
and at the same time retain his membership in his mother Lodge."
"Where a candidate has been rejected the Grand Master has no authority to grant permission for a re-ballot."
He defines dotage thus:
"Dotage is a weakness or imbecility of mind or under~tanding­
caused by old age. Where the weakness or imbecility has progressed
so far as to render the person incapable of understanding the ordinary
affairs of life or at least impairing his faculties, so that he does not
have a clear ~nderstanding of ordinary affairs, he may be said to be in
his 'dotage.' "
He reports a Lodge formed at Nome, Alaska, named Anvil Lodge,
No. 140.

The Correspondence Report reviews California for 1906. The reviewer refers to the great disaster in April and says:
"The Masonic Fraternity arose to the occasion and the teachings of
the Craft, and administered charity to all alike without regard to race
creed or condition. Within twenty-four hours after the catastroph~
had occurred, and while the sky was still red with the flames of the
burning city, the Masons of California, under the guidance of Grand
Master Flint, were organized and actively engaged in their work of
mercy and benevolence."
The reviewer states that California Grand Lodge fixed the sum of
fifty dollars for writing the Report on Correspondence. This is a mistake. The amount was two hundred dollars. The Report was not to
exceed fifty pages.
The reviewer speaks in highest praise of Bro. Davies' ability, .skill
and ex.perience as a reviewer.

WYOMING-1906.
Thirty-Second Communication, Douglas, Sept. 5, 1906.
M. R. Johnston, G. M.
He says:
"Masonry during the last year has had her share of blessings. With
the outer gates well guarded, the inner portals have witnessed the conversion of many good men to our faith and doctrine, and today ·we
stand a tower of strength in the knowledge that this Grand Lodge! has
at its command a mighty army of the truest and best of this young
Commonwealth."
·
·
Referring to the lamented dead, he quotes the beautiful poem,
"Crossing the Bar," which is the expression of Tennyson's unfaltering
faith written in his old age when he was very near the land of sunset,
and already "felt on his brow the breath of the eternal morning."
"Sunset and evening star,
And one clear call for me,
And may there be no moaning of the bar,
When I put out to sea,
"But such a tide as moving seems asleep,
Too full for sound or foam,
When that which drew from out the boundless deep
Turns again home.

''

"Twilight and evening bell,
And after that the dark,
And may there be no sadness of farewell,
When 1 embark.
"For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place
The flood may bear me far,
1 hope to see my Pilot face to face
When I have crossed the bar."
A Committee on Masonic Home reported, saying in part:
"The committee finds, upon examination, that homes of this character are maintained by the Fraternity in many of the States, and as a
rule are carried on successfully and are accomplishing much good.'.' * *
"The committee are also of opinion that in view of the prospective
development of the State and the consequent increase in the price of
lands, that it would be advisable to secure a suitable site at an early
date."
·

Lodge issuing same, with seal of Lodge attached, and the certificate of
our Grand Secretary certifying to the regularity of said Lodge."

REPORT ON . CORRESPONDENCE.

REPORT ON CORRESPONDENCE.

way. The Reviewer who writes these lines ·departs from the above rule
far enough to say that he did · not realize the extent of his task in
reviewing two · years of Proceedings, and postponed its beginqing
until all the Proceedings were received. He then found that the time
in which to get the Report together would not allow the desired
deliberation. Geo. Elliott said, "Through the pass · of By-and-By, you
go to the valley of Never."
In the foregoing Report all Proceedings received have been reviewed without regard. to recognition by our Grand Lodge. It will
be noted that several volumes of Proceedings were not received. 119
volumes were reviewed. It has been a most gratifying if not satisfying work. Three facts gleaned from the Proceedings we repeat : Ireland sent the first message to stricken San Francisco Masons, Illinois has
the most Lodges and New York the most Masons.
The writer believes that the Reports on Correspondence justify the
expense of making and printing them, speaking generally and not referring to the present Report. The methods and procedure of Masonic
organization and Masonic charity and fellowship are not yet perfect.
Upon the improvement of these things are focussed in the many Jurisdictions some of the brightest minds of the world. Advances are constantly being made in administrative methods and a wider spirit of
Brotherhood, in some Jurisdictions, worthy of adoption in others. The
Correspondence Report helps to bring these improvement to the knowledge and consideration of the .Brethren everywhere. They serve to
protect, also, the ancient fabric of Masonry from illy considered innovations, ignorantly proposed or hastily adopted. So too, they assist in
uniting the whole body of Masonry by promoting uniformity in methods
and regulations in the different Jurisdictions and bringing all Masons
into closer fellowship.
.
No one can read the Proceedings of the doings of Masonic Brethren
in all parts of the world, without being both exalted and humbled;
exalted in feeling and in his respect for common human nature by the
evidence of noble . aspiration and high achievement by Masons in different lands, and humbled by the thought of his own failure to live up to
Masonic ideals. For as Hairnet says, "Use every man after his desserts
and which of us would 'scape whipping." These Reports are one of
the links in the chain of Masonic influence by which men living in
widely separated countries, and having different national prejudices are
bound in unity and concord by the Golden Bands of Brotherhood.
Contemplating this Grand Fraternity, having for its object the elevation
of man, we cannot but exclaim: "Hail! Masonry, Hail! Offspring
of the Divine in man! Evangel of Peace and Enemy of War! Proc~ed
on down the ages. The noblest men of earth will acclaim your glorious
worth. and pay homage at your shrine. Hail! and again, Hail!"
Contemplating the majestic Spiritual Temple that our departed
brothers have builded, and which we are striving to build higher,

recalling the memories of the widow's son of Washington1 of Franklin
of t~e multitude of great and good that ~rowd upon the mind, stirred
by high resolves, we pray that we may so live and act as Masons, that
we may be among those
" Im~ortal dead who live again
In minds m.ade better by their presence : live
In pulses stirred to generosity,
In deeds of daring rectitude1 in scorn
For miserable aims that end with self
In thoughts sublime that pierce the night like stars
And with !heir mild persistence urge man's search'
To vaster issues.

• • •••
May I reach
That purest heaven, be to other souls
The cup of strength in some great agony
Enkindle generous ardor, feed pure lov~
Beget the smiles that have no cruelty-·'
Be the sweet presence of a good diffused
And in diffusion ever more intense.
'
So I shall join the choir invisible
Whose music is the gladness of the world."
Fraternally submitted,

Eureka, Cal., Sept. 24th, 1908.

ALONZO J. MONROE,
Chairman.
